04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.name: Traditional bridal costume and jewellery
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.short_description: This set of traditional clothing gives an overall picture of the universally recognized aesthetics displayed in the festive women’s outfits in Macedonia in the 19th century. Bridal costumes worn in the area of Dolni Polog were distinctive for the great number of varied garments they comprised. The costume, consisting of a *fusta*, a kind of undershirt; a *bunda*, a thicker undergarment; chemise; tunic; vest and other garments, was abundantly decorated with embroidery. It was also richly embellished with jewellery and accessorized with distinctive headdress. Even the headdress included more than one article: a fez made of red baize, a hair band called a *votus* adorned with strings of coins as well as a transparent silk scarf decorated with embroidery, fringes and sequins.
04c6becd-fdd7-5c20-9596-b48f8a6ce25a.author: Gordanche Vidinic, ethnologist
keywords: Costume; accessories; headdress; fez; wedding; marriage

05677772-fb33-5d00-af7f-9cb213149293.name: Bottle with depictions of dance and music
05677772-fb33-5d00-af7f-9cb213149293.short_description: This moulded bottle belongs to a group of like examples produced during the seventeenth century in Isfahan, Iran. One side of the bottle depicts a woman playing a tambourine; the other a seated prince watching a woman dance. These scenes of courtly leisure are common to a wide variety of Safavid (1501–1722) arts, including textiles, doors, tilework, and life-size wall paintings in palaces.

06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.name: *The Holy Family and Relatives*
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.description:
This small, sketch-like picture represents the Holy Family with the Virgin Mary and child Jesus in the centre. St. Elizabeth presents young St. John the Baptist, who is handing Jesus an apple, symbol of rule over the world. St. Anne kneels before Jesus. Male family members occupy the background: St. Joseph with a palm branch absorbed in a book, and Zachariah and Joachim, Anne’s husband and Mary’s father.  
The scene is not derived from the Bible but is a story from the Pseudo-Bonaventura. about the Holy Family. The story relates that on their return from Egypt the Holy Family visited a relative, Elizabeth, whose small son, John, we are told, showed great respect for Jesus. Sadler approaches the story in genre fashion, exploiting the individual gestures of all the characters and the evening atmosphere. The painter fully exploits the effects of light and colour, using chiaroscuro to accentuate the family group that spans three generations: Anne, Mary and Jesus. Green, blue, yellow and red tones merge into an almost monochromatic background. The mode of painting on a non-absorbent copper base demonstrates Sadler’s brushwork, along with his trademark facial expressions for the figures.  
The devotional subject, a symbolic triangular composition, and the emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece may have been designed for private worship. It is worthy of note that in the final phase of his studies at the Academia di St. Luca in Rome, Sadler took part in a painting competition which he won with a picture of the Holy Family. The painting corresponds with the Academia’s style, applying approaches associated with Pietro da Cortona, Corrado Giaquinto and Carlo Marrati.  
Sadler’s work, influenced by his studies in Rome, was unique in Moravia. His oeuvre, comprising ceiling and easel paintings, was chiefly associated with central and north Moravia. He was a son of the Olomouc sculptor Filip Sattler and son-in-law of the painter Jan Kryštof Handke.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.short_description: The devotional subject, symbolic triangular composition, and emotional effects of the scene indicate that the piece might have been designed for private worship. The painting is typical of Sadler, a leading Olomouc artist influenced by studying at the Rome Academy.
06a15d7a-7929-5c23-a1f9-e9bf723f6167.method_for_datation: The picture was previously considered the work of Paul Troger. However, the figure types and brushwork confirm that Josef Ignaz Sadler, a prominent Olomouc artist, is author of the work as determined by Vlasta Kratinová.

085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.name: Headdress.
085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.description: The Palestinians of Hebron and the surrounding villages call this type of cap an *araqiyeh*. It is circular with a pointed centre and elaborately embroidered with red and black cross-stitched geometric decoration. Attached to the back of the cap are silver Ottoman coins. The two multicoloured hair-bands (*laffayef*), together with the thin black ribbons fixed to either side of the cap, are modern replacements. This type of headdress has been worn in the Hebron area from the late AH 13th century / AD late 19th century to the present day. During the British mandate in Palestine, the hair-bands (which were used for tying up the hair into a round bun that rested on the back of the neck) were much longer and were made of plaited woollen thread. This headdress was made for everyday use.
085d1bb8-7770-5c15-929d-7644cdd9063f.short_description: The Palestinian women of Hebron and the surrounding villages call this type of headdress an *araqiyeh*. They use the multicoloured hair-bands (*laffayef*) to tie up the hair into a round bun that rests on the back of the neck. The Ottoman coins are for decoration and a symbol of affluence.

08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.name: *Thronus Pietatis*
08d81111-ac94-5a3a-8273-8602b482ae98.description:
The crucified Christ is at the centre of the painting; the Holy Father hovers in the clouds holding up the cross, supported in the lower part by two *putti*. Above His head the Holy Ghost – a dove radiating light – is surrounded by cherubs.  
*Thronus Pietatis* is by the Bavarian painter, Johann Michael Rottmayr, who later moved to Austria and made his name working for the Austrian Monarchy. His first works in Vienna were frescoes in Lichtenstein Palace. He then worked in Melk Abbey and in the Viennese Church of St Charles, Borromeo.  
One of the best-known painters of late Austrian Baroque, his work is characterised by voluptuous figures, strong colours and Baroque gesture. His later works stand apart with calmer movement and paler colours.  
The painting was a commission for the chapel at Valpovo Castle owned by the Hilleprand-Prandau family, by origin from Tyrol. The Prandaus were one of the four most important foreign aristocratic families in Slavonia. The Habsburg Crown granted estates to foreign nobles in Slavonia after the retreat of the Ottoman Turks.

0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.name: Raio Palace
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.description:
A two-storey palace with an irregular quadrangular plan; an internal staircase leads to what is known as the “noble” floor, the main ceremonial floor and where guests were accommodated and the owner slept. There is also an attic. The façade is covered with plain blue *azulejos* (tile panels). The main façade is predominantly horizontal; four windows alternate with three doors at ground level. On the first floor there are six windows and a bay window in the centre, which defines the axis, and has a balcony. On each side of the bay there are two exotic figures.  
The ornamentation on the window frames extends to the main door on the ground floor. Ornamentation of the lintels and door posts, as well as on the curved gables, is typical of André Soares's work.  
The theme is further developed in the façade axis, the ground-floor door having two console motifs, one on each side. The wood carvings and the furniture mirror the console motif.  
The building was part of the program for urban improvement in Braga carried out during the reign of João V in 1760.  
Worth mentioning in the context of Raio Palace, is another work by André Soares that shows the same transitional language between the Baroque and the *Rocaille*, the Malheiros Reimão House.
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.short_description: Urban palace with a trapezoidal plan, two floors and a magnificent Rococo façade.
0b664640-1b19-5212-875c-eb14019b13af.location: Parish of S. Lázaro, S. José, Braga

0cc82bad-3c43-57b4-a06b-eee73296523f.name: Jana o’ Narr Dress
0cc82bad-3c43-57b4-a06b-eee73296523f.description: Dress with wide sleeves and made of white cotton and silk with red, green, and thin, dark blue stripes. The chest panel has striped Kashmir fabric with wavy edges. The neck and shoulders have additional silk cloth and braid work surrounding the chest panel. The sleeves have silk fabric (“bird’s tongue”) in addition to the original cotton fabric colour. The front and back panels have no embroidery work, and the border is done in wavy needlework. This dress is handmade by the women of Tubas (in the Nablus district) for special occasions and weddings. Traditional Palestinian costumes reflect complex social systems that express the owners’ social status, wealth, region and origins through different designs and decorative elements. In this case, both married and single women can wear this dress, but it is usually worn by the wealthy class of women because the fabric is very expensive and not easy to obtain. Wearing this dress is a visual statement that the owner of the dress is from the upper class of society.

0d5820f1-3545-5a87-813f-427001d4dd48.name: *Eliza Bedeković* née *Novak*
0d5820f1-3545-5a87-813f-427001d4dd48.description:
Baroness Bedeković (d. about 1850) married Franjo Bedeković Komorski (1755–1827), a prominent figure in Croatian political life, at the end of the 18th century or the beginning of the 19th century. Elected to the Lower House of the Hungarian-Croatian parliament in Buda in 1790, by 1808 Bedeković was Administrator of Križevci County and, from 1809 to 1825, Grand Sheriff of Bekeš County. From 1825 to his death, he was Grand Sheriff of Križevci County. During his many terms in office, he was a noted Croatian patriot.  
This portrait, probably painted in Vienna at the end of the 18th century, is probably by Johann Baptist Lampi the Elder. Lampi had returned to Vienna from St. Petersburg in around 1797, the year this portrait was finished. Lampi's portraits of this period show meticulous attention to detail in the fine materials and jewellery – details of which abound in this portrait of Baroness Bedeković.
0d5820f1-3545-5a87-813f-427001d4dd48.short_description: This outstanding portrait of Baroness Bedeković – wife of Franjo Bedeković – is probably the work of Johann Baptist Lampi the Elder. Lampi’s portraits of this period show meticulous attention to detail in the fine materials and jewellery – details of which abound in this portrait.
0d5820f1-3545-5a87-813f-427001d4dd48.method_for_datation: The date and possible authorship of this painting were established by study of historical information on the Bedekovićs, stylistic analysis and comparison of other known works by J. B. Lampi the Elder.

0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.name: Emerald-covered box
0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.short_description:
This spectacular gold box has a circular base, vertical sides and a low domed lid. 103 emeralds have been set in the 16 slightly convex rectangular panels of the sides and the 16 curving triangular sections that form the lid. The side panels are carved in shallow relief with cypress trees, their tips curving to the left; the same motif is repeated in the panels on the lid, but the tips of the trees are not curved. Narrow bands of gold frame the emerald panels and a 24-facet diamond is set at the apex of the lid. The base is covered with translucent green enamel and decorated with a central rosette and split acanthus leaves and palmettes.  
Emeralds were mined in Spanish Colombia, exported to Europe and then sent to Ottoman Turkey and Mughal India. Boxes of this type often had a matching tray and they could be used to hold medicines (including opium) or even more precious objects. They are featured in Mughal and Rajput miniature paintings from the end of the 16th century onwards.

0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.name: *Discovery of the Holy Cross*
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.description:
The scene depicts the discovery of the cross upon which Jesus died and the verification of its authenticity. The search for the cross was initiated in 324 by St. Helen, mother of the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, who legalised the Christian faith by an edict in 313. These figures are not represented in this sketch executed for part of a ceiling painting in the Provost Church of St. Hyppolith in Hradisko near Znojmo, owned by the Order of the Knights of the Red Star.  
The discovery, erection and celebration of the cross are arranged in chronological order along the perimeter of the church cupola. In the ancient Roman empire, the cross, tool of the most degrading capital punishment, was designated for slaves and rebels. For Christians, it became the epitome of the redemption of mankind through Christ. The scene is set on Golgotha, where three identical crosses have been excavated. The crosses were laid on dead bodies, and when the genuine cross was applied, the dead person miraculously came to life. In the picture, this is the reclining figure on the left. Maulbertsch's masterly use of light, dramatic chiaroscuro, expressive exaggeration of shapes and rhetorical gesture, is particularly marked in the lifting of the cross. Accents of red and dark blue lend mystery to the picture.  
The final fresco differs from Maulbertsch's sketch only in the decorative detail and colour scheme, which appears less contrasted when seen in large format and makes allowance for the white-green-yellow Rococo stucco decoration of the interior. Josef Winterhalder Jr., later Maulbertsch's most faithful disciple, created his first independent paintings, side altar altarpieces, in this church. The cupola murals are also associated with a sketch by Josef Winterhalder Jr., Maulbertsch's associate and pupil for the *Celebration of the Holy Cross* and the drawings for the cupola paintings (Vienna, Albertina).
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.short_description: This sketch for the mural in the cupola of the Church of St. Hyppolith in Hradisko near Znojmo depicts the discovery of the cross upon which Jesus died and the verification of its authenticity. It exemplifies Maulbertsch’s masterly use of light effects, expressive exaggeration of shapes and rendering of rhetoric gestures.
0fb58449-ced0-5827-ac84-cb93936a6e15.method_for_datation: The Provost of the Order of the Knights of the Red Star signed a contract with Franz Anton Maulbertsch for the decoration of the Church of St. Hyppolith on 9 October 1765. The painter was to start work the following spring. He received 900 gold pieces and was provided board and lodging by the order for himself and his two assistants. The sketch or *modello* was a template for the artist's associates.

10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.name: Tiles of the Buyan Kuli Khan
10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.short_description:
These tile fragments are from the mausoleum of Buyan Qulï Khan in Bukhara. The turquoise glazed tile is decorated with an intricate vine pattern in white. The ornament is not painted, but cut as a relief into the clay using a complex technique.  
These tiles were a part of the decoration program of the mausoleum of Buyan Kuli Khan, who was murdered in 1358. He was the 25th successor of Genghis Khan (1155/62 / 67-1227) and ruled over the Chagatay Khanate empire. His tomb is situated in Bukhara, present-day Uzbekistan, and was covered with tiles both inside and out. The present fragment was initially installed on the outer facade. The Victoria and Albert Museum also possesses several tiles from the mausoleum.
10055861-fa02-5348-9d89-bbe6682bf4ef.method_for_datation: These tiles are from the mausoleum of King Buyan Kuli Khan. They were acquired in 1903 by Justus Brinckmann in Kabebdjan Galleries in Paris.

keywords: Architectural decor; Buyan Kuli Khan; Mausoleum

13a08655-b9b9-5fec-ae88-c539a6b04792.name: Jade pendant
13a08655-b9b9-5fec-ae88-c539a6b04792.short_description: This jade plaque once belonged the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. AH 1037-68/ AD 1628-58). It is inscribed on the front and back with verses from the Qur'an, a scrolling floral design, and two dates: AH 1041 (corresponding to AD 1631-32); and the regnal year 4 (also corresponding to AD 1631-32). The plaque was probably an amulet, based on the selection of Quranic verses and date, which follows the death of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal, suggesting that it was made to help him through this time of grief.

155d1175-57c1-5993-9a33-680636e74497.name: Cosmetic case for a man
155d1175-57c1-5993-9a33-680636e74497.short_description: The craft of lacquer work was widely practised in Iran from the 16th to the 19th century. Master artists in Esfahan or Teheran supplied the lacquer work for the court and the upper circles of society. The main subjects illustrated are: life at court, the legendary history of Iran and religious themes based on the Qur'an and the Old and New Testaments. The mirror and cosmetic case is a nice example of the considerable influence European Baroque painting had on Iranian lacquer work particularly during the Qajar epoch.

16c4b489-744b-54ba-b2f9-e9d429647ac5.name: Bracelet in French Egyptian Revival style
16c4b489-744b-54ba-b2f9-e9d429647ac5.short_description: This bracelet, owned by Princess Paolina Bonaparte (1780–1825), wife of Camillo Borghese, was made by one of the most famous goldsmiths in Paris, Jean Baptiste Claude Odiot, as identified by the trademark on the safety lock of the bracelet. The elegant Egyptian decoration made by hieroglyphics and triangles alternating with little palms is inspired to the book *Voyage dans le Basse et Haute Égypte*, written by Dominique Vivant Denon (1745–1825) during Napoleon’s campaign along the Nile river in 1798 and published between 1802 and 1810. The ancient Egyptian fashion, popular in Italy since the second half of the 18th century, influenced furniture design and works of art following publication of Denon’s book, which popularized a “retour d’Egypte”.

18ce1dd3-9c8e-520a-add7-46441936d12f.name: *The impalement of heads of two trapped Austrian soldiers during the combat at Jaice, August 7th 1878*
18ce1dd3-9c8e-520a-add7-46441936d12f.short_description: This painting depicts a brutal war crime that occurred during the Austro-Hungarian Army's occupation campaign in 1878. On the reverse side of the painting there is a contemporary inscription, which sheds light on the situation: “During the battle at Jaice, Master Corporal Grilec and Private Matko, members of the 53rd Infantry Regiment have been trapped and beheaded. Their heads have been impaled in front of the gate to the river Pliva.” This treatment of prisoners of war was unfortunately not rare during the first weeks of the campaign; it provided a glimpse into a difference in approaches to warfare that would be borne out during the upcoming wars in the Balkans, 1912–13.

keywords: Bosnia; Austrian army; war; warfare

1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.name: Prayer niche (*mihrab*)
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.description:
A prayer niche (*mihrab*) is located in a mosque to show every Muslim the direction of Mecca towards which they pray. The *mihrab* shown here is from the Bey Hakim Mosque, which was endowed by the physician of the Anatolian Seljuq Sultan Kılıç \[Qilich\] Arslan IV (d. AH 665 / AD 1266) and built in Konya. This prayer niche is very similar to others of the same period in its decoration in faience tiles, especially in its combination of calligraphic and decorative elements. These elements have been combined in a variety of ways, resulting in manifold decorations. Borders of differing widths featuring inscriptions and vegetal motifs create unity. Small columns with cubic capitals frame the imagined entrance to Paradise. As was always the case in this period, the lower half of the niche is embellished with geometric patterns and the niche’s upper half by a *muqarnas* (stalactite) vault also covered in geometric patterns. The vault is also framed with geometric motifs. The geometric decoration of the Berlin *mihrab* has an additional 12-star pattern. Raised eight-pointed stars can be found in both spandrel fields. The inscribed areas feature extracts from various parts of the Qur’an. Sura 29 verse 45 is cited on the forefront of the niche: ‘Proclaim what has been revealed to you in scripture and pray. Prayer protects against dishonour and temptation. And truly, to think of Allah is one’s greatest duty; and Allah knows what you do’. The aesthetic unity of the decoration was created by calligraphers and draughtsmen of ornaments in conjunction with the producers of tiles. In terms of colour palette, turquoise, dark blue, black and aubergine were selected. Craftsmen were also responsible for the cutting of the tiles, so that they could be organised into a pattern without leaving any gaps. Tile production in Konya reached its apotheosis around AH 658 / AD 1260, so that, in the AH 7th / AD 13th century, 21 mosques were decorated with faience mosaic.  
  
Click [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hxg1P6Wi4Ro&t=3s) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.short_description: Turquoise, brown and dark manganese faience mosaic was common in monumental Seljuq prayer niches. This impressive niche with Qur’anic inscriptions and arabesque and geometric patterns, once belonged to the Bey Hakim Mosque in Konya, Turkey. It was assembled from fragments and restored parts.

1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.method_for_datation: The prayer niche comes from the Bey Hakim Mosque, which was founded by the favourite physician of the Seljuq Sultan Kılıç [Qilich] Arslan IV (d. 665 / 1266), and which thus dates it to around the mid-7th / mid-13th century.
1b18b5ad-219e-51fb-a044-c41096e34a7f.method_for_provenance: The fragments of this reconstructed niche in Berlin, along with other fragments housed in various cities (Paris, London, Istanbul), formed part of a prayer niche that once belonged to the Bey Hakim Mosque in Konya. Its identity has also been established through early photographs.

1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.name: *Annunciation*
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.description:
This painting was made for the altar of the church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento, a small town near Bologna. The church was part of a recently built college held by the Scolopian Fathers, whose mission was the free education of poor children.  
The simple and clear structure of the painting is perfect for religious instruction. It follows the tenets of religious and profane painting as described in a 1582 book by Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti the Bishop of Bologna.  
Guercino depicts God the Father explaining his mission to the archangel Gabriel rather than depicting the Annunciation. The beautiful angel is a set on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, thus separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.  
Thanks to the Scolopian father Giacomo Bottini the painting “Intangible Dowry for the Instruction of the Poor” was saved from the French requisitions, in 1798.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.short_description: The simple and clear structure of the painting is perfect for religious teaching. Guercino depicts God the Father explaining his mission to the archangel Gabriel rather than representing the Annunciation. The beautiful angel is placed on a diagonal cutting the picture in two, separating heaven from earth. In the lower half of the painting the kneeling Virgin is reading in a bare room, unaware of what is happening above her.
1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.method_for_datation: The commission of the painting for the Church of the Santissima Annunziata (Blessed Annunciate) in Pieve di Cento as well as a series of payments were registered by Paolo Antonio Barbieri, Guercino's brother in the painter's Account Book in 1646.

1ba45d02-7f49-57fa-9238-20be38aa5e1b.obtention: The painting was moved to the council room of the City Hall Municipal Palace of Pieve di Cento in 1924. At that time the church was closed, deconsecrated and converted into a store. Later the painting was moved along with its altar to the church of Santa Maria Maggiore.

1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.name: Prayer rug
1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.description: Outlined on the contrasting green of the central field, the red prayer niche has a stepped arch fringed with hooks along its inner edges. Inside the niche, a floral composition encircled by 12 tiny ewers recalls the mosque-lamp motif. A recurrent motif of prayer rug designs, ewers are traditionally associated with an *aide-mémoire* meant to remind the believer of the ritual ablution required before prayer. The present rug features a main border reminiscent of the so-called Gothic border of 16th- and 17th-century carpets, and, in the upper corners of the main field, stylised vegetal motifs, which show the Western influence on Turkish art. This rather unusual blending of two stylistic sources is illustrative of the two main “forces” with a strong impact on the decorative vocabulary of 19th-century Ottoman carpets: the Turkish tradition and the influence of European art. The bright colour scheme is quite remarkable and its sharp contrasts almost shocking compared mainly to the fine colouring of the Gördes and Kula carpets that reigned supreme on the European market of Oriental carpets at the turn of the century.

1cddac9b-c4c3-5d0f-8b3b-60574b2feaf4.name: Nossa Senhora da Luz (Parish Church)
1cddac9b-c4c3-5d0f-8b3b-60574b2feaf4.description:
The Parish Church in Ponta do Sol has been documented since 1486, when Rodrigo Anes had the church built. It was dedicated to St Mary and had a tomb in the chancel where he wished to be buried, although since then a lot of work has been carried out on the building, beginning in the early 16th century.  
Built on a simple plan with only one rectangular nave and apse, there are two Late Gothic side chapels by the crossing, acting as a false transept. The one on the left has ribbed vaulting, but the chapel on the right has only an entrance arch. The same taste and style are obvious in the delicate lines of the arch of the present Chapel of the Holy Sacrament, with delicate wood carving and a fine representation of phytomorphic elements. The late 16th-century Mudejar-tracery ceiling of the chancel is of particular interest.

2240cc1b-1ee5-59d4-b389-444e8504af89.name: Pendant
2240cc1b-1ee5-59d4-b389-444e8504af89.short_description: The shape of the emerald at the centre of this pendant was determined by its crystallography, which is naturally hexagonal. The later setting was custom-made to complement the emerald's six-sided shape. It is surrounded by variously shaped and sized diamonds in individual gold settings. The top of the pendant features six pearl crowns, each including a large pearl topped with a single green bead. At the bottom of the pendant are three gold loops, from which hang three teardrop-shaped emeralds.

237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.name: Church of St. Lourenço de Almancil
237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.description:
The Pilgrimage Church of St. Lourenço de Almancil is built on pure geometric volumes. Its sober façades with simple, shaped openings are bordered with local limestone. The roof is covered with clay tiles. The exterior, like the cupola, is painted white, influenced by Arab models. There are some cobalt-blue *azulejos* on the exterior walls. The baroque design of the churchyard and doorway are surprisingly elaborate.  
Inside, the gilt, carved wood altar structure of the retable, with its characteristic Solomon temple columns, was built by Manuel Martins, who also carved the arch of the sacristy. Cobalt-blue tiles cover the interior walls, ceiling and cupola, submerging the visitor immediately in their ambiance on entering the church.  
It is probable that Policarpo de Oliveira Bernardes of Lisbon signed the tile panels, indicating his pride in this unique work. Bernardes belonged to a family of painters that specialised in perspective paintings on walls and ceilings. Rather than fresco, tile painting techniques are used here, the designs taken from Andrea Pozzo's book of perspective designs. The architectural *trompe l'œil* was intended to create a fantastic spectacle of Italianate buildings and landscapes which allowed the viewer to forget the earthly space they were in.  
The subject of the tile painting is the Life, Death and Coronation of St. Laurence. Born in Spain, St. Laurence was a martyr in Rome.  
Cobalt blue on a white background shows the European taste in Chinese porcelain at the time. It was first traded in Europe by the Portuguese, and influenced the colours of Portuguese Baroque tile work known as *azulejos*.
237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.short_description: The Church of St. Lourenço (Laurence) of Almancil is an example of Portuguese vernacular architecture. Inside, the walls, ceiling and cupola are covered with cobalt-blue painted and glazed tiles. The walls are adorned with *azulejos* depicting the story of the Life and Death of St. Laurence. The ceiling and cupola are decorated with *azulejos* with Italianate architectural themes in perspective. The carved, gilt- wood high altar retable, in the shape of a pyramidal throne, has massive columns decorated with *putti*, angels, foliage and birds.
237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.bibliography:
Smith, R., "The Portuguese Wood-Carved Retable 1600–1750", *Belas-Artes*, No. 2, Lisbon, 1950.  
Bazin, G., "Morphologie du Retable Portugais", *Belas-Artes*, No. 5, 1953.  
Simões, J. M., *Azulejaria em Portugal no século XVIII*, Lisbon, 1979.

237fec1e-7dde-5bd9-aaa6-983cd97193c0.history: In the 18th century, the Algarve Bishops felt it necessary to increase the religious faith of the locals of Almancil. When water was discovered near a pilgrimage chapel dedicated to St. Laurence, it was seen as a miracle and a sign to rebuild the chapel. The patron of the church was the General Vicar of the Algarve Bishopric District, who also had responsibility for the Brotherhood of St. Lourenço dos Matos, his name and date (1730) are inscribed on the cupola tiles.

25a5389e-c95f-5ff4-9837-134e5233173f.short_description: This exquisite perfume bottle is designed as a gem-set fish, entirely decorated with uncut rubies, emeralds, turquoise and pearls. The tip of the small bottle opens with a screw cap. It was most probably meant to contain perfume or a powder for cosmetic use. Jewelled objects from the Mughal period, such as this bottle, were commissioned for the courtly elite and would probably have been worn attached to a belt or around the neck.

283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.name: Dar Jellouli
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.short_description: With a simple façade and built in a traditional Tunisian style, this house is built around a central square courtyard paved with white marble and with walls covered in blue tiles. The top two storeys are fitted with an ambulatory and wooden railings. The family's wealth is evident from the carved stone framework, ceramics, carved stucco, woodwork, and floors paved with imported marble. The ground floor contains a number of upside-down-T-shaped rooms which attempt to recreate scenes of daily life in 19th century Sfax. The first-floor rooms hold a collection of traditional clothes. Finally, the second floor holds a collection of painting and Arabic calligraphy.
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.history: Located in the heart of Sfax medina, the capital of southern Tunisia, Dar Jellouli once belonged to a rich family from the local nobility. Many members of this family had occupied important positions in the Regency's government throughout the modern period. For example, from 1772 to 1782 Baccar Jellouli was the governor of Sfax. His sons Mohamed and Mahmoud were also members of the city's local government. However, the family made much of its fortune through commercial activities, particularly by owning a fleet of privateer ships. This building was the seat of the local government then from 1939 housed the Centre des Arts under the direction of Lucien Golvin. after independence it became the Musée Régional des Arts et Traditions Populaires.
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
keywords: Architecture; Italian style; stucco; marble

2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.name: Tile panel.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.description: A panel of six wall-tiles, decorated with underglaze painting in the full colour range of the mature Iznik style. Wide green strips with meandering flowering vines form the side borders as well as a pointed-arch motif. The spandrels of the arch are filled with red and white arabesques on a dark-blue background, while the space beneath contains a masterful composition in which naturalistic flowers and large-scale arabesque motifs fill the brilliant white space without overcrowding it. The composition is abruptly cut off at the bottom, indicating that these six tiles formed the upper part of a larger tilework ensemble.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.short_description: A panel of six tiles, executed in the colour palette of the high Iznik style. The decoration features floral decoration beneath a pointed arch. This panel was the top section of a larger panel depicting a niche. It may have adorned an Ottoman palace.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.dimensions: Height 62 cm, width 102 cm, depth 3 cm.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.method_for_datation: Stylistic comparison: the use of green indicates that the tiles must date after the 1570s; while the high quality means they cannot be much later than the turn of the 17th century.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.bibliography: Lane, A., *A Guide to the Collection of Tiles*, London, 1960, p.21.
2aa1cd22-4d00-5e32-bd10-874404e856a3.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; tilework; palatial architecture

2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.name: *The Bazaar at Athens*
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.short_description: The well-known Irish topographer Edward Dodwell toured Greece twice: in 1801 and 1805–6 and he later produced several works on Greece’s scenery, its antiquities and the people’s life. He managed to cover a wide range of Greek subjects and to record faithfully-in both his drawings and his descriptions- various aspects of Greek life and customs. Dodwell’s folio *Views in Greece* (1821) includes an identical image entitled “Bazaar of Athens”, which is obviously based on this watercolour. According to the artist’s description in the text, on the right-hand side is seen a coffee-shop frequented by important people, such as the disdar (e.g. Governor of Athens) depicted in a scarlet gown.
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.author: Tsigakou 1995, 114, fig. 6
keywords: travels; Dodwell; Athens

2d62bc1c-0c3f-50f2-b292-e9b923adbeef.name: Hebron glasses
2d62bc1c-0c3f-50f2-b292-e9b923adbeef.short_description:
Since the Middle Ages, the people of Hebron have manufactured glass which has been characterised by its elegance. Around 1840, glass factories began supplying the households of Palestine with bottles and other glass wares for every day use. For Christian pilgrims, colourful and inexpensive jewellery was produced, which they take back home, either to Western Asia or to Europe.  
At the beginning of the 1990s, the "Hebron glasses" still find rapid turnover amongst tourists and pilgrims. The forms of the hand-blown bottles, cups and little jugs are simple. Their colours are based on precious stones: cobalt blue, bottle green, turquoise, amber yellow, or rose. In the meantime, most of the shops are barricaded, the doors of the houses sealed. A large area of the old city is closed off to Palestinians, and Hebron is divided into a Jewish and a Palestinian zone. The flow of pilgrims and tourists has dried up, and the old "Hebron glasses" have become the trademark of Palestinian identity.
2d62bc1c-0c3f-50f2-b292-e9b923adbeef.method_for_datation: Entry in the TMS digital collection database, documents from the estate of the late collector.

30f8c92a-d056-538d-835c-8f96181283c0.name: Ikhdari Dress (*Malaq*)
30f8c92a-d056-538d-835c-8f96181283c0.description: This *malaq* dress originates in the Al-Khadir area of Bethlehem District, where women embroider it by hand. It is worn only by brides for their wedding day. This dress is made with *Abu Warda* fabric. It has a traditional *malaq* chest panel of flower pot motifs, bordered by two pieces of blue velvet fabric with a bird embroidered on them. The neck and shoulders are made of red fabric. The sleeves are made with silk *hirmizi* cloth in addition to the original fabric of the dress and are embroidered with a Bethlehem clock and a bird. The *banayeq* (side panels) are embroidered with clock and floral motifs in addition to multiple crosses. Traditional Palestinian costumes are characterized by strong emphasis on decoration and colour and are designed from the finest and most expensive fabrics, as shown by this dress.

3277a1c4-6310-5adb-8af8-8874fed7d747.name: *Marija Terezija Oršić (nee Wintershofen)*
3277a1c4-6310-5adb-8af8-8874fed7d747.description:
By birth from a Styrian baronial family, Maria Theresia Wintershofen was extremely well educated. She married Count Antun Oršić (1670/6–1706), a descendant of an old Croatian baronial family who was a cavalry captain and first served in the War of Spanish Succession and then fought against the Turks in Hungary. Maria Theresia and Count Oršić married when they were both very young, before 1695. Soon after, in 1700, he sued her for adultery and for allegedly casting spells on him. Granted a divorce, he took away their three children.  
An unknown, probably Croatian painter has bestowed on this portrait of Maria Theresia something unusual and mysterious, somehow reflecting her strange destiny. The portrait magnificently illustrates various details of female aristocratic dress at the end of the 17th century, notably the influence of French fashion seen in the cap (*fontange)* which is highly decorative and made of ruffled white lace and red ribbons threaded with silver. The colourful dress she wears was typical of the 17th century, richly endowed with pearls and lace. She also wears a small watch, hung on a red ribbon from her waist, accentuating her high social position.
3277a1c4-6310-5adb-8af8-8874fed7d747.short_description: By birth from a Styrian baronial family, Maria Theresia Oršić was very well educated. Maria Theresia and Count Oršić married when they were both very young, before 1695. Soon after, in 1700, he sued her for adultery and for allegedly casting spells on him. Granted a divorce, he took away their three children. The portrait magnificently portrays various details of female dress at the end of the 17th century.
3277a1c4-6310-5adb-8af8-8874fed7d747.method_for_datation: Established through study of the clothes of the subject and her biography.

35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.name: *Woman In Oriental Dress*
35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.short_description: In order to evoke and convey the spirit of the Balkans and the Orient as faithfully as possible, Paja Jovanović meticulously recorded each detail of the interior of a typical Balkan or Eastern house. He also collected props that made up a family’s inventory of furniture (e.g. the hexagonal decorative table to the left), and carefully studied the physiognomies and characters of the men and women he encountered in the southern Balkans, in Egypt, Constantinople, the Caucasus and elsewhere. The precision of draughtsmanship and freshness of colour in this painting by Paja Jovanović ranks it among his more successful works from the mid-1880s.
35645306-e708-561a-ae81-24e697df6d15.author: Petar Petrovic
keywords: Orientalism

35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.name: The Archangel Gabriel
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.description: This icon depicts the Archangel Gabriel turned to the left, indicating that it comes from the Deesis tier of an iconostasis. He wears the *alb* (tunic) of a deacon and the liturgical coat of a bishop. In his right hand, he holds a sphere of light and in his left hand, a rod. The Archangel Gabriel, whose name means “man of God” in Hebrew, has been called the leader of the heavenly hosts. He is associated with numerous biblical events, including the announcements of the births of Mary and John the Baptist, and most importantly, the Annunciation, in which Gabriel proclaimed to the Virgin Mary that she would conceive and bear a son named Jesus.
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2010. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.

39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.name: Set of Icons from a Festival Tier
39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.description:
This set of 12 icons, the only one of its kind in the United States, is believed to be from the Pskov region of Russia. The icons were originally hung on the festival tier of an iconostasis, the partition separating the nave from the sanctuary of an Orthodox church. The festival tier highlights the major holidays of the Orthodox liturgical calendar. This set includes the following images:  
  
1\. The Meeting of Anna and Joachim  
2\. The Nativity of the Virgin Mary  
3\. The Nativity of Christ  
4\. The Presentation of Christ  
5\. The Transfiguration  
6\. The Raising of Lazarus  
7\. The Crucifixion  
8\. The Three Marys at the Sepulchre  
9\. The Descent  
10\. The Ascension of Christ  
11\. The Holy Trinity  
12\. The Feast of Pentecost
39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.obtention: From the De Wijenburgh Collection. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Idonen Galerie, Germany, in 2012. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Life of Jesus

3c48fcf6-1014-510b-ae78-07b7a91937a4.name: Basto del Diavolo (Urban Gate)
3c48fcf6-1014-510b-ae78-07b7a91937a4.description:
The so-called "Basto del Diavolo" (Devil’s packsaddle), located at the intersection of Via Appia Antica and Via di Vallericcia, is probably the Roman Porta Urbica (Urban Gate) built in the Republican period and which provided access to the Forum of Aricia. It consists of an arch in *opus quadratum* with armilla (a second set of ashlars) incorporated on a wall on the sides. The Eastern face shows signs of the 19th century’s restorations. During the excavations of 1980, *basolato* (a type of Roman paving) of Via Appia Antica was found under the arch and later interred again.  
(Bibliography: E. Lucidi, 1796; G. R. Florescu, 1925; R. Lefevre, 1977; M. Lilli, 2002; M. Leoni, 2008)

3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.name: Frescoed architectural fragment from a bathhouse.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.description:
A frescoed architectural fragment that once formed part of a bathhouse, consisting of a niche with a pointed arch. The imagery within the niche portrays a figure, executed in black and red watercolours against a white background, executed in the fresco technique. The subject is a seated youth – who might have been a prince – and who holds a cup in his hand. He is wearing a loose robe-like garment, which is decorated with red vegetal motifs. His upper arms are encircled by two bands, and his head is covered by a pleated turban. A complete circular halo appears around the youth's head, perhaps to emphasise his status. He wears a scarf placed around his back, the two ends emerging from under his armpits and then left hanging down, suspended in mid-air. Two parts of the youth's hair can be seen beneath the turban, one in the front and the other at the back.  
The niche is framed by an arch composed of bead-like roundels. The fresco itself resembles paintings found in Samarra, Iraq in terms of both the figures; the shape of the heads and the circular halo, for instance, as well as in the repetitive decorative motifs; the frame in the form of an arch, for example. In addition the implementation of style is far from realistic, and leans more towards the decorative, with clear Persian influences. The Fatimid frescoes are not too different in form, style, or thematic content from depictions executed on metallic lustre ceramics, which were being produced in Egypt during this period. It is possible to study the pictorial representation on this architectural fragment by comparing it to similar Fatimid-period examples executed on various media: ceramics, some wooden pieces and on many textiles. Furthermore it is interesting to consider the role of painting itself as a distinctive decorative component of the applied arts during the Fatimid period.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.short_description: Baths were buildings of importance in the Islamic world due to their role in purification and hygiene. The walls of bathhouses were commonly decorated with frescoes, like the example we see here.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.method_for_datation: Painting on all the applied arts is a distinctive feature of the Fatimid period, it also makes comparison with other paintings of the period a useful means of dating an object.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.method_for_provenance: Fustat was narrowed-down as the place of production for this architectural fragment as the piece was discovered *in situ* in a Fatimid bathhouse.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.obtention: Archaeological excavations undertaken by the Centre of Arab Antiquities in 1932 revealed the presence of a Fatimid bathhouse in the region of Fustat. Some of its constituent parts, including this architectural fragment, were transferred and registered as acquisitions of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo in 1934.

3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.name: Villa Falconieri, fresco decoration in the Spring Room
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.description:
The interior was decorated immediately after the architectural extension, and was executed between 1668 and 1680 (possibly 1672–77), according to a single plan inspired by the cycle of the seasons and the ancient outline provided by Ovid's *Fasti*. The *trompe l'oeils* decoration is by Grimaldi, who after the death of Pietro da Cortona in 1669 directed some of the artwork using Cortona's pupils. The works harmoniously incorporate a range of different elements: the image of a garden in which the trees act as theatre wings, giving depth to the space and reflecting Grimaldi's scenographic culture; the rich vegetation surrounding the space in a sort of idealised isolation; the statues with garlands of flowers and the painted fountains and architecture – the whole marked by classical references and flights of fancy, filled with springtime symbols of flowers and fruits.  
The vault—painted by Ferri, Pietro da Cortona's principal pupil—shows *Flora* intent on scattering flowers and accompanied by the winds, in line with traditional iconography, stylistically characterised by graceful rhythms in polished forms with a classical style, a precursor to the shift towards Rococo.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.short_description: The Spring Room is part of a decorative cycle dedicated to the four seasons. Different elements representing the seasons merge harmoniously in *trompe-l'oeils* painted on the walls filled with springtime symbols of fruits and flowers. The vault depicts *Flora*, intent on scattering flowers and accompanied by the winds.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.method_for_datation: Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Rufina Falconieri*, Rome 2008.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.bibliography: Guerrieri Borsoi, M. B., *Villa Rufina Falconieri: la rinascita di Frascati e la più antica villa tuscolana*, Rome 2008 (with bibliography).
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.history: Villa Falconieri was erected on terracing originally created for a building from the Roman era. Built for Alessandro Rufini, a *Cameriere Segreto* (secret manservant) to Pope Paul III Farnese (1534–49), the villa originally had a square, fortified appearance with angular towers. Some decoration remains from this period, including the unicorn from the *impresa* of the Farnese family. It then passed to the Sforza family – related by marriage to the Boncompagni family – where it became a favourite meeting place for the papal court of Pope Gregory XIII Boncompagni (1572–85). It was at this time that Frascati became the holiday destination for the papal court and Roman nobility, reviving a tradition of *otia* (combining rest with meditation) thanks to its wholesome surroundings, abundance of water and the vicinity to nature. In 1628, ownership of the villa passed to the Falconieri family, which later—probably using a design by the architect Francesco Borromini (1559–1667)—entrusted Camilo Arcucci (1617/8–67), in partnership with Francesco Massari (1665–1705), with the task of expanding and converting it. The architect included the existing structure—a porticoed façade between two *avant-corps*—into an entirely new spatial concept, creating in the upper storey an ample concave *exedra*, which enabled optimum use to be made of the light, both in the contrast between voids and in-filled sections and of the alternating concave and convex forms, highlighted by the blind arches that frame the windows and decorate the entire façade, as was his preference.
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.architects: Giovanni Francesco Grimaldi (1606, Bologna – 1680, Rome), painter and project leader; Ciro Ferri (1633, Rome – 1689, Rome) pupil of Pietro da Cortona (1596, Cortona ­– 1669, Rome)
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.institution: National Institute for the Evaluation of the Educational System of Instruction and Training (INVALSI)
3ebd113a-5f55-5cc8-b28a-28fb23a87b8f.author: Laura Indrio
keywords: Perspective painting, *trompe-l'oeil,* illusionistic, floral, fresco

4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.name: *The Annunciation*
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.alternate_name: *La Madonna del Bell’Angelo* (*The Madonna with the Beautiful Angel*)
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.description:
This altarpiece was originally commissioned for the Fioravanti chapel in the former St. Bartholomew church. It was inaugurated in 1632. In 1647 the Barnabites fathers commissioned the same painter to complete two smaller side paintings with episodes of the life of the Virgin (the *Adoration of the Child* and the *Dream of St. Joseph*) and asked for some retouches to the *Annunciation*. In 1685 the church was inaugurated and the three pictures were moved to the fourth chapel in the right side aisle, where they remain today.  
The altarpiece soon became renown as the *Madonna del Bell'Angelo* (the Madonna with the beautiful angel) for the beauty of the announcing angel.  
Albani builds the picture by juxtaposing the standing Madonna, nearly indifferent to the annunciation, against the Angel that is bursting from the dark closed room with luminous shades of yellow. Following the angel, a cloud of cherubs and putti rolls from heaven in a chaotic but lively invasion. The picture mixes the naturalistic lesson of the Carraccis with the round lines and the vivacious movement of full Baroque style.
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.short_description: This painting was made by Francesco Albani, one of the pupils of the celebrated Carraccis. These three cousins strongly contributed to the Baroque revolution in Bologna and throughout Europe. Albani is a very pleasant painter. He tells the story of the *Annunciation* in a captivating way, showing the Madonna as a princess full of grace and self-control and the heavenly court bursting with enthusiastic life.
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.holder: Church of Saint Bartholomew and Gaetano
4166b82f-2a5c-5946-adbb-0669c7207263.obtention: The object is still preserved in the original location.

45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.name: Coupled-Column Prayer Rug
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.description: A version of 17th century Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs very popular in Hungary was the "column" rug, in which the *mihrab* (prayer niche) is divided into three fields by three, four or eight columns. The most common is the six-column version, considered by many to have the most beautiful design of 17th century Turkish rugs. Their general characteristic is a *mihrab* (prayer niche) whose background colour is red or ochre (rarely ivory or blue), divided into three parts by slender columns in a 1+2+2+1 distribution. The rug’s ochre *mihrab* (prayer niche) is supported by six narrow columns, dividing it into three fields. The spandrels have a blue and red arabesque decoration on an ochre field, and the crenellated frieze above has straight-stem flowers growing out of it. The design of the peak field and the frieze are not sharply delineated. Rounded cartouches of alternating colour run along the border; the outer border has a row of leaves of alternating orientation and the inner border is decorated by leaves and flowers strung along an undulating stem. In May H. Beattie’s classification, the rug is an early, type I Coupled-Column Prayer Rug.
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.dates: First half or middle (?) of 17th century
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.dimensions: Height: 191cm (+2cm x 27cm fringe), Width: 119cm, Knot density: 1,482/dm2
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.obtention: The rug previously belonged to Arnold Ipolyi (1823-1886), Bishop of Nagyvárad, who collected it in Transylvania. It was exhibited in the 1914 'Transylvanian' Turkish Exhibition in the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts by the Bihar County Museum of Nagyvárad (Oradea, Romania). The rug entered into the inventory of the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts in 1962 as 'Item in store, of unknown origin'.

4bd11f30-7eb1-584b-9175-3069c058941f.name: A pair of still-life paintings: Confectionery and Pottery and Confectionery and Flowers
4bd11f30-7eb1-584b-9175-3069c058941f.description:
This is one of two still-life paintings belonging to the Anselmo Braamcamp Freire collection by Josefa d' Óbidos. The influence of the Flemish, Dutch and Andalusian schools, which Josefa d' Óbidos adapted to her Naturalist genre to create her own distinct style, is clearly visible here. The painting reveals an essential simplicity, in which the central details are the confectionary, the pottery and flowers, and it is this very simplicity allied to the artist's delicate technique as well as a wide colour palette, that transform these works into silent and realistic worlds of living objects in all their serenity.  
It is worth mentioning the use of a range of whites which in its subtlety adds to the vivid realism of the paintings and heightens the awakening of all five senses that is so redolent of Baroque Art and so characteristic of this artist.  
Another approach to these paintings is to regard them as allegories of Christianity and the monastic life. Symbols such as the bread, the silverware and the pots are connected to festive occasions and feasts like the Eucharist. Ceramics are associated with the daily rituals of the town of Óbidos.  
It is also possible to establish a connection with the Baroque discourse of the Counter-Reformation in which the gesture and behavioural excesses of human nature stand out, in contrast to the principles and values of purity and simplicity. Valuable objects and luxurious embroideries are represented together with white roses, representing the spirit of patience and red roses, associated with spiritual martyrdom.  
Exploiting her knowledge of symbols and the significance of plants, the artist turns each detail into a symbol of reality and man's moral and spiritual values. Thus, the cherries and roses symbolise happiness, maternal love is suggested by the carnations and eternal life is characterised by the butterfly.
4bd11f30-7eb1-584b-9175-3069c058941f.short_description: Josefa d’ Óbidos' still-life evokes the Counter-Reformation's Baroque ideas in which Man's gesture and behavioural excesses contrast with purity and simplicity. Details like bread, cakes, silver and embroidery symbolise human values in contrast to the flowers, representing spiritual values.

4d95a12b-05ca-5d85-bfaf-474830773927.name: Monkeys taunting a lion
4d95a12b-05ca-5d85-bfaf-474830773927.short_description: This single-page drawing of Monkeys Taunting a Lion is on a folio from a dispersed album. Ruled off in a pale blue frame decorated with golden trees, flowers, birds, and insects and trimmed down to a narrow frame ornamentation, the drawing is outlined in black and has line detail with some light grey shading. The subject of this drawing is not determined by a narrative text. However, it may have been inspired by an animal fable such as *Kalila wa Dimna* (Kalila and Dimna), which has a long tradition in Iran.\[1\] The artist was also likely influenced by the influx of Chinese styles, patterns, and motifs in the early 15th century.\[2\] The vogue for Chinese drawing and painting may have been the inspiration for this drawing, similar to the wild landscape with the struggling animals and dragon.

4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.name: Pair of earrings.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.description:
The Fatimid period is distinguished by the development of precisely executed objects with high levels of decorative concentration. This is evident in wood, metal, and gold objects from the period.  
This pair of earrings is made from a gold web that is hollow from the inside. Each individual earring is in the form of a bird carrying in its beak a small gold ball. The loop provided for hanging the earring from the ear of the wearer connects the head of the bird with the rear of its body, making the arch of the bird's back straddle the earlobe.  
The earrings were made from gold wire carefully soldered together and accentuated with a few gold granules. The granule technique creates a light and hollow whole that is both aesthetically and practically pleasing. This technique was also used to create spherical or bi-conical beads that were then strung together into necklaces and other kinds of jewellery.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.short_description: This small but meticulously executed pair of gold earrings is a prime example of dexterity in the technique of filigree. Birds were a favoured ornamental motif and the filigree technique maintained the lightness of the subject without compromising their opulence.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.dimensions: Length (at longest point) 3.5 cm, depth (at deepest point) 1.21 cm.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.method_for_datation: The production of this type of hollow, woven gold object was well known in the Fatimid period, specifically in the first half of the 5th / 11th century.
4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.method_for_provenance: Although purchased in Raqqa, the method of production described above was associated with multiple sites in Egypt and Syria, such as Cairo and Aleppo. It is difficult to determine, therefore, a definitive provenance.

4df720fc-29e6-59ab-9430-1945b274992e.author: Mona al-Moadin

4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.name: *Marketplace, Morocco*
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.short_description: This imposing oil painting shows a caravan apparently leaving the gate of a North African city, perhaps Fez, with much commotion going on on either side of the camels and their guides. Although the title of the painting suggest a market scene, in reality little trading activity can be seen apart from an old hooded man sitting next to a large basket with shoes on the right. On the left a group of African men and a little child in a burnous admire the skills of a snake charmer, while his monkey next to him looks on intently. In the background, large numbers of men, apparently both of Arab and Berber origin, and dressed in a variety of traditional dress, walk along or stand together in groups conversing, oblivious to the camels, donkeys and horses moving inbetween them. Ferenc Eisenhut was an Austro-Hungarian painter, known for his monumentally conceived genre scenes of Eastern life and vistas. He was the only internationally acclaimed, Hungarian Orientalist painter.
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis

54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.name: Tile from ceramic inscription panel of the Dome of the Rock.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.description:
A tile forming part of a ceramic inscription panel that once decorated the exterior octagonal pinnacle of the Dome of the Rock. Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–73 / AD 1520–66) commissioned the panel while renovation work of the Dome of the Rock was being carried out, in around AH 969 / AD 1560. Each tile is 25 cm high by 25 cm long, and the whole inscription panel is 160 m long. The panel is decorated with a long Qur'anic inscription consisting of the complete text of the chapter “Ya-sin” (Chapter 36). The text is written in the Ottoman *thuluth* script in white against a dark-blue background. The inscription is interspersed with vegetal decoration consisting of intertwining spiralling stems, with blossoms and leaves. The tiles have a characteristic simplicity, and are of fine colouring and very detailed workmanship. The tiles represent an early example of Ottoman ceramics, used generally in architecture during the period, and more specifically in the Dome of the Rock. Buildings were often panelled with ceramic tiles during the Ottoman period, in fact, such tile work is a distinguishing trait of Ottoman contributions to the restoration and renovation of holy places, not only in Jerusalem but also in places such as Mecca and Medina.  
The Islamic Museum have acquired all sections of this inscription panel which was removed from The Dome of the Rock in 1960 during restoration works. The Museum has since housed and preserved the inscription panel as a witness to the first stage of ceramic-tile panelling on the outer walls of the Dome of the Rock. It is worth noting that previous to these tiles, the outer octagon of Dome of the Rock was covered with a glass mosaic, which had deteriorated badly due to age, until Sulayman the Magnificent ordered the removal of the damaged mosaic and replaced it with these tiles.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.short_description: A glazed tile from a band that wrapped round the exterior octagonal pinnacle of the Dome of the Rock, ordered by Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent during his renovation of the Dome. It is written in *thuluth* script in white against a dark-blue background. The verses are interposed with vegetal decorations.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.dimensions: Length (of a single tile) 25 cm, width 25 cm, depth 3 cm.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production for these tiles. This is supported by historical sources indicating the presence of a workforce and Ottoman ceramic tile-making kilns in the area.
54153ed8-09be-518c-8b1b-5c34eb3644e6.obtention: The piece was transferred in 1960 from the Dome of the Rock to the Islamic Museum.

55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.name: Painted chest
55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.short_description: The main façade of the chest is adorned with a composition of flowers, branches and fruits in curvilinear compartments, while the corners depict female figures flanked by columns. The interior of the lid shows a landscape with five male figures: a man with a European garment sitting on the ground observing another figure dressed in European clothes, two figures on horseback with Ottoman costumes and a European traveller. The panels in the style of rocailles that adorn both the main and the side views of the chest, the compositions of fruit and flowers and the soft colours refer to the prevailing influence of the rococo style that is dominant in the frescos of the mansions of Lesvos the late 18th century. Both the structure of the mansions and the decorative repertoire follow Ottoman aesthetic as these were by influenced by European art but blending baroque, rococo and neoclassical styles.
55e346ff-6f0e-5e17-90fe-1d309d2d7056.author: Xenia Politou
keywords: furniture; rococo; baroque

5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.name: Panel of tiles.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.description:
A comprehensive group of ceramic tile panels in the form of a pointed arch. Apple-green is used for the background of the peripheral panels while a dark-blue dominates the central panels. Both the floral ornamentation and the calligraphic inscriptions are coloured white and carefully stencilled in black. The technique used to apply the colours is underglaze painting.  
These fine Damascene Ottoman tiles were found in the tomb chamber of the Mustafa Lala Pasha mosque, located above the window that overlooks the cemetery. The three lines of *thuluth* script translate as follows:  
(1) Protector  
(2) May the mercy of the Lord be upon him in every moment  
(3) Everything is mortal except for the countenance of God, He has the power of rule, to Him you will all return.  
The year AH 998 / AD 1590 was written in numerals in two locations between these lines. The spaces surrounding the inscription, as well as the space between the words, are filled with finely executed stylised vegetal motifs. The depiction of multiple flower varieties swaying in the breeze recalls the extent to which Chinese styles influenced the repertoire of Islamic ceramics. The choice of *thuluth* script for the calligraphy is a favoured ornamental script in tile work because of its monumental letter proportions and its curvaceous painterly quality.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.short_description: Ottoman style underglaze painted tiles made in Damascus display the painterly quality of *thuluth* calligraphy on a background of spiralling floral motifs.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.initial_owner: Probably a governor of Damascus during the reign of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 981–1003 / AD 1574–95).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_datation: The inscription on the panel includes the date of its completion, 998 (1590).
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.method_for_provenance: The underglaze technique is consistent with local Syrian techniques of ceramics manufacture and distinctive from the Ottoman overglaze method. During this period, Damascus was a flourishing tile-production centre. It is therefore likely that the tiles were produced in Damascus.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.provenance: Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha, Damascus, Syria.
5691ad24-fe0c-597d-8ca1-206be34877d4.obtention: The tile panels entered the Museum in 1919 when the mosque in which these tiles were originally located was demolished to make room for the Suq al-Hal, the Cardamom Market.

56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.name: Prayer carpet '*sajada*'
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.short_description: A highlight of the Khanenko Museum's Islamic collection is an Ottoman carpet dating to AD late 17th–first half of the 18th century. The carpet belongs to the traditional type of "*sajada*", or prayer, carpets, with composition based on a stylized picture of *mihrab* - a prayer niche in a mosque indicating the direction where Muslims turn during the prayer. The composition and motifs of the carpet, particularly the central niche coloured in plain dark blue and crowned with arch of an acute stepped shape as well as a peculiar geometrized carnation pattern above and below the niche, suggest that the item was manufactured in workshops of Giordes or Kula, two leading centres of Turkish carpet-making in the 17th–18th centuries. Numerous narrow ornamental borders that fringe the central arch add a specific elegance to the piece of art.

5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.name: *Saint Charles Borromeo Administers the Sacrament to the Plague-Infected*
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.description:
This excellent oil sketch (*bozzetto*) is linked to one of Caspar Franz Sambach's early works, the interior decoration of the parish church in Sloup, Moravia, a grand ensemble of magnificent frescoes and altarpieces, which were completed between 1751 and 1754. The Esztergom *bozzetto*, and a slightly larger and more complete version in Breslau (Wrocław; the Narodowe Museum), were produced for the side altarpiece dedicated to St. Charles Borromeo. The composition follows Pierre Mignard's painting for the high altar of the Church of San Carlo ai Catinari in Rome, probably by way of an intermediary engraving.  
Charles Borromeo, the archbishop of Milan at the time of the great plague of 1576, fought heroically against the epidemic; following his canonisation in 1612, he was accorded reverence similar to that of the medieval plague saints. His cult outside Milan strengthened in Rome at first, and then, through Borromeo family connections in Salzburg, it grew further during the reign of Charles VI spreading throughout the Habsburg Empire.  
Born in Breslau (Wrocław), according to local studies, Sambach worked in Vienna from 1740 in the workshop of the sculptor Georg Raphael Donner. He trained as a historical painter at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, becoming a member in 1759, a professor in 1762 and director in 1773. His fresco and altarpiece paintings were influenced by other Central European painters, the likes of Paul Troger, Michelangelo Unterberger and the younger Franz Anton Maulbertsch. Sambach was a skilful ornamental artist and painted his own architecture; producing the figure inserts that imitate reliefs on his frescoes, as well as on his canvases depicting *putti,* making use of the methods learned from the works of the Austrian, sculptor Georg Raphael Donner. In Hungary, the high altar and ceiling frescoes, together with the altarpieces of the Jesuit church in Székesfehérvár (1749–50), preserve his early, relaxed style. The Esztergom colour sketch, a loose and vivid composition that shows only the lower part of the altarpiece, can be considered as an autograph version (*ricordo*) made by the master.
5a5065ff-617c-5f77-81aa-546635c333e8.short_description: The Silesian, Caspar Franz Sambach, also worked in Hungary (Székesfehérvár, Buda and Nagykanizsa). One of his most important works is the interior decoration in the parish church in Sloup, Moravia, including the altarpiece commemorating Charles Borromeo. Two oil sketches of Charles Borromeo's altarpiece are extant; the one seen here is considered to be an autograph version (*ricordo*) of the Breslau (Wrocław) study.

5a8a244d-67e0-5d59-8dde-4569de053291.name: *General Junot Protecting the City of Lisbon*
5a8a244d-67e0-5d59-8dde-4569de053291.description:
In the context of the French invasions of Portugal Domingos Sequeira established friendships with the officers of the Napoleonic army at an early stage, as was the case with Count Forbin, an officer and amateur painter. Due to these contacts Sequeira was commissioned to produce an allegorical painting to celebrate the role of General Junot in protecting the city of Lisbon. Sequeira's action was perceived as an acceptance of the ideals of the occupying enemy and he was persecuted and his work condemned. Later on, after the defeat of the French, it was difficult for Sequeira to exonerate himself, something that has still only partially been achieved.  
Three groups in the open-air on the top of a hill populate the foreground. Standing in the main central group is General Junot who wears military uniform and is turned towards a young woman who represents Lisbon; she is supported by Religion and Genius of the Nation. To the left in the mid-ground are two men; with only their bare torsos visible they represent Mars annihilating Neptune, and symbolise France and England respectively. On the opposite side, two female figures suspended mid-air move towards the central group; they represent Ceres and Minerva and are symbols of Abundance and Wisdom. Above them an eagle hovers, its huge wings outspread. The landscape is a great plain that stretches out until it reaches the sea. At mid-distance, a large army with knights on horseback advance in formation. In the background a fleet is anchored near the beach. The sky, heavy with clouds, creates a gloom that covers the greater part of the painting. The sky opens out, however, to clearer and more luminous tonality towards the horizon over the sea.
5a8a244d-67e0-5d59-8dde-4569de053291.short_description: The French General, Junot, offers protection to the city of Lisbon, supported by the personifications of Religion and Genius of the Nation. The central composition is flanked by Mars and Neptune (representing France and England) and on the opposite side, Ceres and Minerva under a huge figure of an eagle.
5a8a244d-67e0-5d59-8dde-4569de053291.initial_owner: João Allen Collection, Porto, acquired in 1827 from the painter himself.

5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.name: The Battle between the Novgorodians and the Suzdalians
5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.description: This icon type, among the first to depict an event from Russian history, illustrates the 1169 battle in which the Suzdalians besieged the city of Novgorod. During the siege, Archbishop Ilya of Novgorod ordered that an icon of the Mother of God be brought out from the Church of the Transfiguration to give the Novgorodians courage. According to legend, the icon was displayed on the city walls where it was struck by a Suzdalian arrow. The icon miraculously began to weep, and through the intercession of the Mother of God, the Novgorodians defeated the Suzdalians. This image is particularly rich in its narrative and compositional details.
5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 1995. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.name: *Still life with Crabs, Pitcher, Glass, Loaf and Mouse*
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.description:
Izbighy Veres of Kassa (Košice) was one of the most accomplished painters of the period in Hungary. According to sources, he executed several commissions in Kassa (Košice), and a number of his still life paintings are in Slovakian and Hungarian collections today. Indications of the Hungarian origins of this painting are evident not only in the signature, but also in the blue-white lead-glazed jar; in addition, the loaf of bread is similar to that seen on a supraport painting by him in Koháry Castle at Szentantal (Antol). In another painting in the Xantus János Museum, Győr, Izbighy arranged a heap of crawfish on a plate in a similar way.  
Up until the beginning of the 20th century, discussion of Izbighy Veres' still life paintings was primarily in terms of their symbolic meaning. In this particular painting, however, this is hardly a major consideration as, clearly, it is influenced by the 17th-century still life genre of Austria and south Italy and, considering its style and spirituality, is certainly related to three works of the Austrian “Burgher paintress” Anna Maria Punz (Österreichische Galerie, Vienna), though this one by Izbighy is of an earlier date.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.short_description: The signed work of István Izbighy (Izbigi) Veres, a painter from Kassa (Košice) shows the influence of Austrian and south Italian still life painting, in particular the work of the “Burgher paintress” Anna Maria Punz. His other works may well have symbolic meaning but symbolism is a minor consideration when considering this particular painting.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and the date established by stylistic analysis.
606d3d8f-c123-5583-829c-0f993f3625e5.obtention: Transferred in an exchange from a Swiss private collection to a private collection in Karinthia, Austria.
