60d42b24-3acf-5ae0-ab4f-e3aae453f313.name: *Still-life with Calligraphic Panel*
60d42b24-3acf-5ae0-ab4f-e3aae453f313.short_description: Feyhaman Duran was particularly interested in portrait painting and went to Paris in 1910 through the patronage of the Egyptian Prince Abbas Halim Pasha to further his studies in this genre. He greatly profited from the teaching of Paul Richet, professor of anatomy in the School of Fine Arts in Paris. He also attended the Julian Academy where he learned a great deal from Jean-Paul and Albert Laurens. In 1913-14 he worked in the Cormon studio in the School of Fine Arts. Although devoting most of his time to portrait painting, Feyhaman Duran also did paintings of flowers and nudes, but he was definitely most interested in the portrayal of people, and he had very little time for non-figurative painting.
keywords: Painting; Feyhaman Duran; orientalist painters; still life

6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.name: Moroccan House in Linderhof  Palace Park
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.short_description: The king had considerable alterations made to both the outside and the inside of the house in keeping with his own lavish tastes. Jean Perron, a sculptor in Paris who had organised the purchase for Ludwig II, also acquired the rich furnishings appropriate for an ornamental setting such as tables, chandeliers, tabourets, mirrors and vessels, none of which have been preserved. Numerous skilled workers and artists were involved in the dismantling, rebuilding and altering of the house.The entire colour scheme was changed with an abundant use of gold, and individual rooms were furnished with costly materials. Coloured glazing “in the Moorish style” and a tessellated floor were introduced to add to the oriental character of the house.
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.type: Pavillion; Park building in Linderhof Palace Park
6129ee64-d66a-53c2-9b9c-8ac38a87b8b9.history:
When the rebuilding of the “Moorish Kiosk” in the Linderhof park undertaken by order of Ludwig II was completed at the beginning of 1878, it evidently reawakened the king’s interest in buildings in the Islamic architectural style.  
The pavilion, acquired at the World Exhibition in Paris in 1878, was remodelled inside at Ludwig II's request and originally built on the Stockalpe near the Austrian border. The "Moroccan House" had already also been shown at the International Exhibition in Vienna in 1873 and had been built for this purpose in Morocco. The wooden building, acquired by a private individual after the king's death, was bought back by the state in 1980 and was reconstructed in the palace park in 1998.
keywords: King Ludwig II; Linderhof Palace; Ettal; Moorish style; Romanticism; gardens

685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.name: Wooden Sideboard with Mother of Pearl Inlay
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.short_description: This tall, intricately carved sideboard consists of two parts, the mirror section with intricately carved openwork and mashrabiya ornamentation enhanced with mother-of-pearl inlay, and the narrow table section decorated with similar elements and with its four front legs supporting an elaborate system of lobed arches. the sideboard is further enhanced by religious inscriptions, some of which seem to suggest a Christian context. Sideboards and other European-style furniture were unknown in the Middle East until the second half of the12th/ 18th century. By the 13th/ 19th century, the urban elites in Ottoman cities enthusiastically imported domestic furniture from Italy, France and England or bought locally-made hybrid pieces that combined European and traditional Islamic elements like the item shown here. Many European entrepreneurs like the Italian Furino Brothers, based in Cairo, set up shop in Ottoman cities and specialised in this so-called Arabesque style, especially fashionable for furniture.

6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.name: Niche or prayer carpet
6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.description: This is the first carpet purchased by the MAK after its founding. Together with numerous embroideries, it was bought in 1868 from the Mechitarist congregation based in Vienna and formed the start of the MAK’s internationally notable carpet collection. It supposedly came via Iran to Vienna. If one compares it with the pictorial carpets containing landscapes and pairs of birds, one clearly recognises the further development of the Mughal style: away from the naturalistic depictions towards the detailed *mille-fleur* design of the centre field and the integration of vegetal elements into the architecture, such as the flanking cypresses. The carpet displays a flora made of fine Pashmina wool, which allowed especially detailed lines.

6c0ec863-e0e7-5b08-9c07-4fe22fc9d7ae.description: This advertisement shows that the influence of Orientalism was telegraphed to the public as a synonym for exotic places, buildings and dresses. This advertisement also could be related to the Russian ballets of Sergéi Diágilev.

6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.name: *Die Himmelfahrt Christi (Ascension of Jesus Christ)*
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.description: The extremely elaborate series of tapestries known as the "Old Passion" was purchased for the Dresden court during the reign of Duke George the Bearded (1471-1539). The tapestries held in the collection at the Palace in Dresden, which numbered around 230 items in 1565, not only constituted a valuable financial asset but also functioned as a symbol of state power. In addition to the four tapestries preserved in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, which were woven in Brussels between 1524 and 1528, the series probably also included six further scenes from the Passion, which were presumably destroyed during a fire in the Palace in 1701. The tapestry depicting the Ascension of Christ, which was produced in the Brussels workshop of Peter van Edingen van Aalst shows the Son of God being transported upwards on a phenomenon consisting of light and clouds carried by angels. He raises his arms in a gesture of blessing over his disciples, who are left behind on the Mount of Olives. The exaltation of Christ symbolises the end of his earthly existence as he takes his seat at the right hand of God. It is presumed that the designer of this composition was Bernard van Orley, who was clearly influenced by the graphic works of Dürer and Raphael. Although this tapestry is still in keeping with the traditional style of 15th century painting, the monumentality of the figures and the realistic depiction of the landscape already reveal the influence of the Renaissance.
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.obtention: The first mention of Flemish tapestry in Dresden dates from an entry in the 1565 inventory of the "Tapetzerey Gewelbe" in the Palace. As part of the series known as the Old Passion, which originally included ten tapestries, this work probably came to the Saxon court during the reign of Duke George the Bearded (1471–1539).

6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.name: *Lamentation of Christ*
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.description:
The canvas dates from the Flemish painter's first trip to Rome (1602), and is contemporaneous with his first Roman commission: the paintings for the Sant' Elena Chapel in the Church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
The work was probably done for Cardinal Montalto and did not become part of the Borghese collection until 1827.  
The scene shows the Lamentation of Christ according to the Gospels. In the centre of the picture, conforming to the dramatic style typical of Baroque art is the body of Christ in a bold foreshortened position, stretched out on an ancient sarcophagus and surrounded by different characters. Mary supports him with the shroud (in which he is wrapped) while looking to the heavens, where beams of light pierce dark clouds, accentuating the almost nocturnal setting of the subject. John the Evangelist, the young apostle loved by Jesus, stands opposite the elderly Joseph of Arimathea. The right side of the painting shows two female figures: one the pious woman, almost hidden, and Magdalene, in full light, in the act of drying her tears. The high drama of the composition and the richness of the colours perhaps come from the famous *Deposition* that Caravaggio completed for the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella (1602–1604). The painting nonetheless reveals clear references to Dutch Mannerism, combined in this case with classical models copied by the artist in Rome, with brilliant colours and diagonal compositions taken from Venetian and Emilian painting.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.short_description: This work was painted by Rubens during his first stay in Rome (1602). He matched Barocci's colours, the dense brushwork of the late Titian, and the roman statuary and the light and shadow of Caravaggio. The Baroque genius had blended, in an absolutely original way, this tradition with new experimentation.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.name: *The Suicide of Lucretia*
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.description:
The *Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque artist, Carlo Francesco Nuvolone, or Nuvoloni (as he is known to some authors) whose work belongs to the Milanese Baroque school. The painting, done in the latter part of Nuvoloni's career when he achieved work of a higher quality, is less cloying and has less pathos than earlier works. Taught by the Mannerist painter, his father, Panfilo Nuvolone (1581–1651) at the Ambrosiana Academy in Milan, he went on to study there with the well-known painter G. B. Crespi aka *il Cerano* (1557–1632). Influenced by Guido Reni, Francesco was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia. His work is characterised by pleasing colour, expression, sensuality and composed pathos. Francesco painted portraits, religious compositions and historical subjects. Other works by him are found in Milan (the Pinacoteca Ambrosiana and the Pinacoteca Brera), in churches in Pavia and Varese, in Piacenza (Museo Civico), in the Dresden Alte Pinakothek and in some chapels in Lombardy.  
The subject of the painting is Lucretia, daughter of the Roman senator, Lucretius Tricipitinus, and wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. Following her rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, she committed suicide in 510 BC, which spurred Roman discontent with tyrannical rule and led them to proclaim a Republic.  
The dying Lucretia lies diagonally in the foreground. Her torso unclad, she has a mortal wound to her breast. Her greyish flesh colour is in contrast to the rich folds of red drapery that cover her knees, and in harmony with the white and green fabric of her clothing. An older woman bends over her curved body wrapped in a dark cloak, from which her lit face and the palm of one hand poke out. Lucretia and the older woman create a simple, closed composition with characteristic composed Baroque ardour and exaltation. Lucretia, symbol of chastity and of tragedy at the same time, is the victim of her own beauty. In the mid-ground on the left-hand side of the picture, from the deep shadow alongside a pillar, peer the faces of three old men. On the opposite side, the composition opens out to a landscape, bounded with clouds, within which are two Roman soldiers. The painting is composed of light and cold tones, with a silvery range.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.short_description:
*The Suicide of Lucretia* is the work of the Baroque painter from Lombardy C. F. Nuvoloni, known by some as Nuvolone, who was born in Cremona. Taught at the Ambrosiana Academy by his father, Panfilo, he went on to study with G. B. Crespi. Inspired by the painter Guido Reni, he was nicknamed Guido di Lombardia, living and working in Milan, painting portraits, religious and historical subjects.  
The theme of this painting is the suicide of Lucretia. Lucretia was the daughter of the senator, Tricipitinus, and the wife of the Roman consul, Tarquinius Collatinus. In 510 BC, following Lucretia's rape by Sestus Tarquinius, son of King Tarquinius Superbus, the Romans ousted the king and declared a Republic.  
The painting shows the half-naked body of Lucretia in her death throes. Leaning over her is an older woman, while in the background three old men peer out. In the background landscape, Roman soldiers are barely discernable. In this painting, the artist depicts the tragedy of a beautiful woman with a composed ardour characteristic of the Baroque. He painted Lucretia in a cold and light tonality, richly lit with a silvery light; in the dark mid-ground, in contrast, are barely discernable figures.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.method_for_datation: The attribution to Nuvoloni by Dr. Grgo Gamulin in 1961 was through stylistic analysis and comparative material, as well as by comparison with the other established works of the painter.
6f38889e-696b-5ed9-a574-a215465cbd09.obtention: The painting was once in the Museum of Modern Art in Dubrovnik among the works of the old masters. In 1978, the Museum of Modern Art and the Dubrovnik Museums agreed, with the approval of the Ministry of Culture, to give the works of the old masters (16th–19th centuries) to the Dubrovnik Museums, specifically to the Dubrovnik Cultural History Museum. Today the painting is on permanent display on the first floor of the former Rector’s Palace.

7030a53b-c9dd-5d53-9b01-c53042f5dec9.name: Stand for Sweets
7030a53b-c9dd-5d53-9b01-c53042f5dec9.description:
The sweets stand was made in the factory of Nacko Janković & Son in Jagodina in the last decade of the 19th century. It is made of pressed, partially transparent, partially opal blue glass. The stand consists of a plate with a raised, wave-pattern rim set atop a high stem attached to a smaller base, decorated with radial rings and stars.  
Serbia’s movement toward the European way of life during the 19th century included the acceptance of new cultural models. Everyday life, especially in urban areas, changed with the introduction of novelties such as the use of porcelain and crystal sets to the culture of dining. High quality glass could be seen at first only in formal cultural settings. Later, imported glass products were augmented by the more accessible domestic glass products, whose design relied on the imported products. Thus, the Nacko Janković & Son factory had a wide range of items for sweets consumption. In addition to various types of fruit, cakes and sweets stands, candy bowls and saucepans, the Nacko Janković & Son factory produced various dishes for the traditional *slatko*, a special delight prepared from fruit, bowls for sugar or "*ratluk*", sweet Turkish delight, etc.
7030a53b-c9dd-5d53-9b01-c53042f5dec9.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.

706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.name: Miniature 'Mi'raj (the Miraculous Ascension) of Prophet Muhammad'
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.short_description: Mi'raj is the scene of the Ascension of the Great Prophet Muhammad to Heaven to the throne of Allah. The iconography of the scene has become established in the Iranian painting tradition since the late AD 15th century. The composition of Mi'raj, together with the poetic dedication of God and His Prophet, traditionally opened manuscripts of historical, biographical and poetic works of classical Persian literature. In the centre of the scene we see Prophet Muhammad riding the fantastic animal Boraq, a mare with a woman’s head. Muhammad is traditionally depicted with a large flaming halo around his head. His face is covered by a veil, probably added to the picture later. In front of the Prophet, we see the Archangel Jabriel showing the way. Above the Archangel there is a lion, the heavenly personification of Ali, the first righteous Imam of the Shiites. Angels with gifts fly around the Prophet. Between the figures against the blue sky, golden "Chinese" clouds abound. The miniature subject combines two important Islamic legends. The Qur'anic Al-Isra (Night Journey, Surah 17) recounts the Prophet's magical night flight from Mecca to Jerusalem. The Al-Mi'raj (Staircase), narrated in hadiths, is the story of Muhammad's miraculous ascent to Heaven to the throne of God.
706091ba-1c94-588c-882c-871fe5fdaca3.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by V. Krachkovskaya (publication, 1926, origin and date).

78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.name: *Muqarnas* decoration
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.short_description: Developed in Iran, the *cuerda seca* technique was designed to produce multicoloured glazed tile decoration quickly, efficiently and cheaply. It was introduced to western Anatolia in the Hegira early 9th century / AD 15th century, probably by a group of Iranian master artists, whose work decorates the Ottoman royal mosque complex in Bursa known as the Green Mosque. An important example of *cuerda seca* tilework, possibly from the same building complex, is this ceramic revetment moulded in the form of *muqarnas* (stalactite- or honeycomb-like elements used as decoration in Islamic architecture). It is painted in a typical colour scheme of dark blue, turquoise, white and yellow. *Muqarnas* elements such as this one were produced in modular units and later set into place on building façades.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.method_for_datation: The color scheme and cuerda seca technique relate this *muqarnas* element to the tile decoration of the Green Mosque Complex, Bursa, built between 822-827 Hegira / AD 1419–1424.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.method_for_provenance: The glazing technique and colors are comparable with the tile decoration in the so-called Green Mosque Complex in Bursa.
78426513-4220-51b8-99aa-4f7ba05f6c3a.obtention:

7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.name: Qarawiyyin Mosque.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.description:
A simple oratory of about 100 m2, the original mosque was made up of four naves parallel to the *qibla* wall, a courtyard, a *mihrab* and a minaret.  
In the AH 5th / AD 11th century, the Almoravids enlarged and enriched it with elements borrowed from Andalusian ornamental style fashionable at that time: plasterwork sculpture, *muqarnas* (stalactite) domes, sculpted marble capitals, epigraphic and geometrical floral motifs, etc. The *mihrab* dates from this time, as do the earlier domes. The mosque is embellished with *kufic* inscriptions and floral compositions that are reminiscent of Islamic art in Spain.  
During the Almohad era, AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries, the Qarawiyyin was again endowed with new ornaments and practical additions such as the latrines in the north of the building and an underground warehouse on the northeast side used to store oil, mats and other material from the mosque. To bolster the monument's existing hydraulic infrastructure, a pool was constructed and water was channelled from one of the wells of the *medina* ('Ayn Farmal). Lighting was provided by a large chandelier in the ribbed dome of the axial nave and by bells along the central aisle that were imported from al-Andalus and transformed into chandeliers.  
The Mosque reached its heyday during the Marinid era (AH 7th–9th / AD 13th–15th centuries) with its 270 pillars forming 16 naves of 21 arches each, 15 large doors reserved for men and 2 small doors for women. With its 509 lamps, the large central chandelier weighed 1,763 pounds. The building could accommodate 22,700 people in its halls.  
Unlike most mosques in the Muslim west, the naves of the Qarawiyyin are not perpendicular but parallel to the *qibla* wall, which suggests an oriental influence (probably the Great Mosque of Damascus).  
The minaret, which is as old as the original mosque, was built in freestone and subsequently covered with plaster and carefully polished whitewash.  
The Sa'dids (AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries) took inspiration from the Alhambra in Granada for the two magnificent pavilions of the *sahn* (courtyard), which is evident in their layout as well as their decoration and architectural elements.  
The 'Alawids were responsible for restoring the chandeliers, the walls and pillars.  
The Qarawiyyin was also a real university, playing a major role in the diffusion of knowledge and the training of the intellectual elite. The Marinids provided two libraries and organised the institution and the teaching programmes, with 140 teaching posts throughout the establishment and the *madrasa*.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.short_description: It was in the AH 8th / AD 14th century that the simple oratory founded in the AH 3rd / AD 9th century by Fatima al-Fihriya in Fez old town, having become a Friday mosque, reached its apogee with its 270 pillars, 17 large gateways, a library and enough space for 22,700 worshipers. A university of great prestige and an important spiritual centre, Islam's most celebrated scholars came from Córdoba and Damascus to study or to teach at one of the Qarawiyyin's 140 chairs, located throughout the establishment or in the town's different *madrasas* and mosques.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.method_for_datation: Written sources such as the *Rawd al Qirtass* (The Mausoleum of Writing) by Ibn Abi Zara al-Fassi and the *Jana Zahrat al-Aas* (Myrtle Flower) by al-Jaznaï enable us to date the foundation and extensions (see Bibliography).

7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.name: *St. Andrew*
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.description:
Figure type and a diagonal X-shaped cross identify the subject of the work as St. Andrew, a fisherman from Galilee and Christ's first disciple. The elongated figure, with an S-shaped body and one foot forward, is sketched in light outline. The artist's attention is dedicated to the modelling of body volumes and the rendering of a system of draperies in an elaborate network of parallel and crossing lines of varying density and intensity.  
Josef Winterhalder Sr. came from a family of sculptors in Schwarzwald. After studying at the Vienna Academy he settled in Moravia, in Olomouc and Znojmo. At the beginning of the 1740s, shortly after a trip to Dresden, where he studied sculptures by Balthasar Permoser, he obtained a large commission in Náměšt nad Oslavou. Between 1740 and1744 he created a series of 20 larger-than-life statues of saints and angels in shell limestone for the Náměšt Bridge, one of three of the kind surviving in the Czech Republic. Winterhalder invited the sculptor Alexander Jelínek, member of a renowned family of sculptors from Velké Meziříčí, to collaborate with him. Winterhalder produced several drawings associated with the commission, three of which are preserved in the graphic art collection at the Moravian Gallery. The drawings represent St. Joachim, St. Andrew and St. Michael. Brilliant specimens of Baroque drawings for sculpture they demonstrate the essential part the artist Paul Troger played in shaping Winterhalder's drawing style. Similar drawings have also survived for the decoration of the Dominican Church in Brno.  
The drawings of Josef Winterhalder Sr. significantly contributed to the further dissemination of Paul Troger's influence among artists active in Moravia. Winterhalder employed his drawings, for example, in the training of his nephew, the future painter Josef Winterhalder Jr. Winterhalder's drawings were also used by other artists, such as Johann Lucas Kracker.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.short_description: The drawing refers to the decoration of the bridge in Náměšť nad Oslavou, one of the few of its kind to survive. Josef Winterhalder came from a family of sculptors in Schwarzwald. After studies at the Vienna Academy he settled in Moravia, first in Olomouc and later in Znojmo.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.method_for_datation: The drawing probably comes directly from the estate of Josef Winterhalder Sr. Its style corresponds with the sculptor’s manner of work.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.obtention: The drawing, acquired as early as 1863, is part of a series possibly passed directly from the estates of Josef Winterhalder Sr. and his nephew, painter Josef Winterhalder Jr. In all probability, the series later came into the property of the sculptor Andreas Schweigl and later the archivist Jan Petr Cerroni, Moritz Wilhelm Trapp and Emil Kořistka, all of whom were curators at the Brno museum.

821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.name: Rosette.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.description:
Decorative rose patera or rosette in sculpted plaster composed of ten petals in blue on a red background. All that remains of the blue is a tiny trace on the edge of a petal. The central part would have been painted in yellow, as other plaster fragments discovered at the same place were painted in blue, red and yellow. The disappearance of the colour is due to the natural effects of light and air.  
This rose patera was no doubt just one element belonging to a plaster frieze that featured three colours (blue, red and yellow); or perhaps, as is affirmed by Marçais, it was placed on the cornerstone of an arch.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.short_description: Sculpted plaster piece representing a ten-petal rosette, originally painted blue, around a corolla, which may have been painted yellow, all on a red background. The colours have not survived well. This rosette would have been part of a multicoloured plaster frieze.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.method_for_datation: It was found in the Dar al-Bahr of the Qal'at Bani Hammad, which dates from the 5th–6th / 11th–12th centuries, according to Kitab al-Istibsar: 'The Banu Hammad built some important constructions in the *qal'a* … including \[the palace\] known as Dar al-Bahr, at the centre of which was a vast basin'.
821bf5d1-f03e-5876-835a-d807cdb83a6e.method_for_provenance: From the report of the De Beylié excavation, 1909.

825bbc31-2ea9-5983-a4b5-235679be04cb.name: Niche of al-Uweyna Mosque
825bbc31-2ea9-5983-a4b5-235679be04cb.short_description:
The 10th century AH/16th century AD is considered the richest period for production of *mihrabs* (mosque niches), known for the work of masters like Abdullah bin Qasim al-Manahi and the family of Mushmil al-Manahi who lived during this time. Talib bin Mushmil al-Manahi, who built the niches of the Grand Mosque in Nakhl and as-Saruj Mosque in Samail, also made the niche of al-Uweyna Mosque in 970 AH/1562 AD. The niche on display is covered with geometrical decorations, fine inscriptions, quotes from the Holy Qur'an and inscriptions documenting the names of the builder, designer and the patron.  
  
The Islamic *ash-shahadatan* (Declaration of Faith) is written in *kufic* inscription at the upper part of the niche and the outer rectangular frame contains 30 seals with floral decoration. The niche itself sits in the cove of the inner frame with a rectangular shape above it baring inscriptions in two triangles and three plates of glazed Chinese pottery in the centre.
keywords: Mihrab; Niche; Declaration of Faith; kufic; Geometric

8416e828-5b8b-5b06-93d0-9f518e17c49a.name: The Emigrants
8416e828-5b8b-5b06-93d0-9f518e17c49a.short_description: Angelo Tommasi is a naturalistic painter, influenced by Courbet’s realism, and he played an active role spreading the technique employed by the Macchiaioli. The monumental painting *The Emigrants* shows a common situation in Italy after the unification process. The dramatic theme of overseas emigration is vividly depicted by the packed crowds at the Port of Livorno, of people who have resigned themselves to their fate and the expectation of embarkation. The painting's extraordinary dimensions contribute to an illustration of the theme of Italian emigration on an almost epic scale.

84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.name: Traditional dress for a *shaykh* or *shaykha*
84d4fca3-e4d2-596e-bea2-0a5eda7a5ccf.short_description: Featured here is the traditional dress for the *shaykh* and *shaykha* of the Keserwan district. The *kubran* is an embroidered jacket (with or without sleeves) made of silk or velvet. The *gumbaz* is a long dress or coat embroidered with gold or silver and sometimes adorned with semi-precious jewels. It consisted of three panels and was split on either side of the body, beginning from the hip area. Other components of this traditional attire were a *mentiene* (blouse), the *shirwal* baggy trousers, a velvet or satin cape with gold or silver embroidery, and a long belt called a *shamle* or *zunnar* made of silk or cashmere depending on the season, and which was wrapped around the waist or hips.

85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.name: Horizontal ground loom
85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.description: This useful tool has been used since the Neolithic age. A horizontal ground loom is a simple arrangement of four pegs tied in place. The warp (vertical) threads are wound onto the sticks and tied in place. The loom has a heddle, batten, jacks, a warp beam and a shed rod. The weaver works the weft (horizontal) threads, by hand, through the stretched out warp. A shuttle is used to pass the wool.

86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.name: *Death of St. Joseph*
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.description:
St. Joseph, the patron saint of a happy death and of Austria, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. Many 18th-century artists embraced the subject, for instance Carlo Maratta in 1676, and it was adopted in around 1730 by Francesco Solimena, Giambattista Pittoni, Giambattista Piazzetta and Francesco Trevisani (Rome, S. Ignazio). Trevisani's work became a template for a number of pictures around the theme of St. Joseph, including Paul Troger's *Death of St. Joseph*. Korompay's Christ is very close to Troger's figure of Christ in the painting mentioned, especially in his mirror-image gesture. While in Troger's picture (and in the majority of the examples given) St. Joseph is lying on a bed, Korompay depicts him kneeling, supported by an angel. The motif was probably not the artist's own; he might have come across it in a reproduction print of an artwork from the Italian *Settecento*, a period that favoured motifs of drooping figures – whether they were saints or Christ himself – supported by angels. Pittoni employed this relationship between two figures in his *Ecstasy of St. Theresa*, Ricci in *Landscape with St. Mary Magdalene and an Angel*, and Trevisani in *Christ on the Mount of Olives*. The motif, however, can also be found in Troger's and Franz Anton Maulbertsch's early oeuvres.  
Korompay developed the composition of the main figures in a shallow foreground, placing them within a group of appealing gesticulating figures that provide a link with the second figurative layer represented by an angel and *putti*.  
The artist's segmented brushwork accentuates the illusion of the scene's ascending tendency. The palette features a rich scale of subtle warm shades blending into one another – from deep red to pale pink and mauve – making up the colour base of the picture. Korompay off-set this colour scheme with the pasty tones of lemon yellow and yellow-green seen in Joseph's gown, and the cold blue of Jesus' cloak, contrasting with his red undergarment.  
The painting was a template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, which is preserved there to this day.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.short_description: St. Joseph, patron saint of a happy death, became a principal subject of altarpieces around 1700. The composition, based on paintings by F. Trevisiani and P. Troger, is the template for the side altar altarpiece at the Parish Church of St. James, Brno, preserved to this day.
86d80b99-bfa0-554b-a10c-63e31c9639bb.method_for_datation: Korompay created seven pictures for the Church of St. James, a fact recorded in the sources and reflected in the paintings of Franz Anton Palko – a painter of altarpieces and a distinguished portraitist active in Brno and south Moravia.

889d2d1f-9798-5292-a324-1416cf3c2c35.name: Azakhana-e-Zehra
889d2d1f-9798-5292-a324-1416cf3c2c35.description:
This magnificently built *azakhana* (Shia shrine) is located on the south bank of the river Musi, in the Darul Schifa area of historic Hyderabad. It is symbolic of the easy religious coexistence of Muslims and Hindus in the city. The shrine was built by the Sunni *Nizam* Mir Osman Ali Khan (1886 – 1967) in honour of his Shia mother Amtul Zehra Begum. Architect Zain Yar Jung was commissioned to design a monument representing the power and glory of the kingdom.  
  
The Shia shrine is a place of mourning for Shia Muslims. It houses *alams*, or battle standards, and is regularly visited by Shia devotees. In *Muharram*, the first month of the Islamic calendar, it also hosts religious gatherings called *majalis*. During this month the monument is transformed into a space for solemn meditation. Worshippers visit the shrine to commemorate the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima and son-in-law Ali, and his grandsons Hasan and Husain, the latter of whom died in the Battle of Karbala in 680 A.D. (10 *Muharram* in the year 61 A.H. of the Islamic calendar).  
  
Azakhana-e-Zehra was built in the Qutb Shahi architecture style. It has impressive outer elevations, and the interior of the structure is magnificent. The square building is topped by circular cupolas and divided into three sections by pillars. It also has two courtyards. The outer courtyard is overlooked by balconies and spans the distance from the entrance gate to the platform holding the main building.  
  
The interior of the monument is painted in a rich green accented with black and gold, and the names of the martyrs of the Battle of Karbala have been inscribed on the ceiling. The entrance can be unimposing, but leads to a vast open space with balconies and intricate decorations, with a platform directly across from the door.  
  
The teak ceiling of the shrine is an imposing 13 metres high, and stands without supporting pillars. The upper balconies have a *jaali*, or decorative screen, for women mourners attending gender-segregated religious gatherings. The walls are decorated with verses from the Quran and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, written by master calligraphers. During the *hijra* or *hegira* that marks the Prophet Muhammad’s migration from Mecca to Medina, *alams* made of gold and precious stones are displayed here.

894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.name: Church of Worship and Basilian Monastery of Máriapócs
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.alternate_name: Greek Catholic Church of Worship and Monastery
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.description:
The Church of Worship of Máriapócs has a transept and two towers on the west façade; the sanctuary is oriented east. It has three ridged turrets on the roof and the vestry is on the south side.  
The date of construction and the names of the builders are commemorated on a chronosticon above the main gate, above which there is a mosaic representing the Madonna (*Theotokosz*). Beside bishops, many of the church’s patrons are lying in the crypt.  
The main red marble altar was a gift from Count Pál Forgách Bishop of Nagyvárad (Oradea) in 1750; the two preparation altars (in the sanctuary with the main altar); its pulpit (carved and gilded with the statue of St. Michael the archangel above); the painting of the Apostle Paul below the baldachin, with paintings, *Christ and the Samaritan Woman* and the *Seed-Sower*, and the structure of its iconostasis (with a Rococo balustrade and crowned with a cross; the pictures of which date to 1896) are also 18th century.  
There are two side altars: on the north side, the Altar of the Virgin Mary (1943–1944) designed by the Franciscan monks of Pécs, now houses the the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs”. The south altar, known as the Altar of the Heart of Jesus, holds a cross relic. The Great Altar of St. Basil is at the same side of the church.  
The sanctuary wall paintings, by Manó Petrasovszky, depict King St. Stephen (Szent István) I offering Hungary to the Virgin Mary with the first martyr St. Stephen, patron saint of the Diocese of Hajdúdorog, and Hungarian saints and pilgrims. The stained-glass windows were made after designs by Petrasovszky between 1944 and 1945. Other wall paintings are by József Boksay (1943).  
The two-storey rectangular Baroque monastery is connected to the church via a suspended corridor.
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.short_description: The Church of Worship in Máriapócs is one of Hungary's most important places of worship particularly for the Greek Catholic community living mostly in eastern Hungary. Up until 1950, the church was maintained by monks from the next-door Basilian Monastery, which was consecrated in 1756. The interior of the church along with the furnishing, much of which dates to the 1780s, has been renovated several times during the 19th and 20th centuries. A copy of the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” was placed in the church in 1707. Since then, this miraculous image has wept twice, attracting numerous other miraculous events to Máriapócs.
894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.method_for_datation: Based on written and visual sources, stylistic and field research.

894da41a-1e64-5cc8-a198-b729d87b6c64.history:
The Church of Worship and Monastery of Máriapócs is a highly significant place for the Greek Catholic Church. Pócs first gained significance in 1696 when in a small, wooden Greek Catholic church in Pócs a group of soldiers witnessed a devotional image, painted in 1676, weeping.  
The original “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” was commissioned by László Csigri judge of Máriapócs as a votive painting in gratitude for his release from Turkish captivity. István Papp, the younger brother of the local Greek Catholic pastor Dániel Papp, painted the picture but the judge could not pay him on completion. Lőrinc Hurta and his family subsequently purchased the painting and donated it to the church. Following the first act of weeping, Emperor Leopold I had the painting transferred to Vienna, where it was finally placed in St. Stephen's Dome on 11 September 1697, the day the troops of Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated the Turkish armies at Zenta (Senta). The people of Vienna related the triumph to the miraculous power of the “Mary of Pócs”, which Leopold I confirmed in his bull issued to Pócs in 1701.  
Belief in the power of the painting led Leopold I to support the people of Pócs in their fundraising efforts to erect a new church in 1701. Later, Charles VI Emperor gave permission for construction of a church, and the settlement of Greek Catholic Basilian monks in Pócs; Count Ferenc Károlyi donated a large sum of money towards construction as well as his entire Pócs estate.  
Construction began in 1731 at the personal expense of Bishop and Apostolic Vicar György Bizáncy Gennadius, but was halted when the bishop died in 1733.  
István Simon Olsavszky and Gábor Blazsovszky renovated the deteriorating walls before Bishop Mihály Mánuel Olsavszky continued the building programme and consecrated the church in 1749. The foundations were laid and the sanctuary walls erected by 1748.  
In 1749, Bishop Olsavszky received permission from Queen Maria Theresia to establish the Basilian Monastery and the independent bishopric of Munkács (Mukachevo). By 1751, the foundation stone was laid and part of the monastery was complete, so the monks from Munkács (Mukachevo) moved in. The whole building was consecrated in 1753.  
By 1756, the church was complete.  
The Greek Catholic Vicar of Pócs addressed a petition to the emperor requesting that the “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs” be returned. Leopold I promised that a replica would be donated to the church in his written transcript addressed to István Telekessy Bishop of Eger, but in the end, Telekessy commissioned an Austrian artist to paint the copy in 1707, which arrived to Pócs in the same year.  
The paintings of the iconostasis (replaced in 1896) are by Mihály and Tádé Spalinszky (Tádé was also a Basilian monk) of Polish origin between 1785 and 1788. Its gold-plated wooden structure was probably made by a craftsman from Eperjes (Prešov).  
In 1943, the miraculous “Weeping Mary of Máriapócs”, which hung above the Royal Door of the iconostasis, was moved to a side altar in the north wing, then in 1946, on the 250th anniversary of the first weeping, it   was moved to its present location.  
The marble main altar was made in the 18th century; the towers of the church in 1856, and the new bronze gate of the church completed in 1991 for the visit and mass of Pope John Paul II. Pope Pius XII gave the Church of Worship of Máriapócs the title Basilica Minor in 1948.  
The church was cared for by Basilian monks until the dissolution of the order in 1950. The monastery then became a care home, and 10,000 volumes from the library were removed, along with valuable furnishings and items of worship from the church and monastery, which were scattered among various locations. Renovation of the church and monastery began in 2008.

89f36061-aab4-567a-ad9a-8b9204d45732.name: Ar-Ribash, *Kitab al-'Izz wa'-manafi' li'l-mujahidin fi sabil Allah b'aalt al-hurub wa'l-madafi'* ('Book of Glory and Advantage for Those Fighting in the Holy War with Artillery and Cannons for the Glory of God')
89f36061-aab4-567a-ad9a-8b9204d45732.short_description: This manual titled ‘Book of Glory and Advantage for Those Fighting in the Holy War with Artillery and Cannons for the Glory of God’ ( *Kitab al-'Izz wa'-manafi' li'l-mujahidin fi sabil Allah b'aalt al-hurub wa'l-madafi'*) was written by Ar-Ribash (in Spanish Rivas or Rives) around 1630-32. It was translated around 1638 from Spanish by Ahmad b. Qasim b. Ahmad b. al-Faqih Qasim b. ash-Shaikh al-Haghari al-Andalusi. According to the colophon, this copy was completed by the scribe Muhammad Khuja, the son of translator Ahmad b. Qasim, in 1050 AH / 1641 AD in the city of Tunis, Tunisia. The manuscript was published by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall in 1811, so it must have entered the Austrian National Library before this date. Interestingly, from a cultural and historical point of view, this North-African copy is an example of European technical knowledge disseminating into the Arab world. However, hadiths were added to the text, and landscape background as well as the figures of European artillerymen were omitted from the 38 half- to full-page technical drawings. Fewer than a dozen copies exist, and their dates of manufacture range from the middle of the 17th to the late 18th century. Another example of this manual is a directly or simultaneously copied manuscript located in the National Library of Algiers in Tunis (no. 1511). The author copied the text of the book *‘Plática manual de artillería’* by Luis Collado (Milan 1592) partly verbatim, and partly in an abridged form. The same manuscript as well as C. Lechuga’s *‘Discurso de la artillería’* (Milan 1611) served as models for the technical illustrations.

8c623df6-63e7-59cd-8751-f117d02f1259.name: Necklace
8c623df6-63e7-59cd-8751-f117d02f1259.short_description: This necklace comprised of ten turquoise stones which are fashioned into oval and polygonal shapes. The turquoise stones are connected using enamelled gold rosette spacers. The inscriptions and decorated foliate motifs on the turquoise stones are inlaid with gold. The *nasta’liq* inscriptions recall popular devotional phrases dedicated to a special and important individual. Turquoise or *firuzeh* which means victory is a national colour in Iran. It was the preferred colour of the interior and exterior of domed mosques, as it symbolises the heavens.

901912af-e2dd-5692-a2e7-be09e9e75334.name: 'Abaya-style dress
901912af-e2dd-5692-a2e7-be09e9e75334.description: This ‘abaya style dress incorporates a variety of fabrics sourced from all over the world brought together into a vibrant yet harmonious piece.   Colourful Indian and Southeast Asian textiles in the form of silk ikats and brocaded sari borders sit alongside embroidered suzani panels from Central Asia and plain coloured textiles sourced in the United Kingdom or the Middle East.  Designed by Thea Porter for Thea Porter Couture, this garment harked exoticism.  In line with fashion trends of the 1970s, designers such as Porter looked to Middle Eastern, South Asian and Central Asian textiles for inspiration, incorporating them into their designs. Such bright textiles with their vibrant colour combinations, textures, and bold patterns spoke to notions of travel to exotic destination, highlighted exposure to different cultures, and in an era of synthetic fibres, placed emphasis on natural materials and the handmade.  Born in Jerusalem but having lived in Damascus and Beirut, Porter introduced her Western clientèle to voluminous Arab-style over-garments such as ‘abayas and thawbs.    Her loose shapes and her innate understanding and choice of fabrics appealed to many with Porter being credited with bringing the bohemian look to London catwalks.
901912af-e2dd-5692-a2e7-be09e9e75334.obtention: Gift of Venetia Porter in memory of Thea Porter (formerly in the collection of Honor Frost).

90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.name: Catholic Collegiate Church of St. Lawrence and St. Stephen
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.description: The building is composed of three nave and two choir bays without transept. The space’s uniform appearance is largely due to the barrel vault extending along its entire length and the uniform sequence of aisles. Here, drawing on early North Alpine Jesuit buildings, the Italian scheme of a hall with side aisles has been executed in the form of a pilaster construction. During the course of the stuccowork the entablature, which originally extended over the side chapels, was restricted to the choir-loft parapets. Above this transverse, barrels cut into the main vault. As a result of the choir lofts at entablature height the interior still echoes with the closed atmosphere of an Italian-style hall with side aisles. Although the interior design originates from two phases, the overall impression is one of great uniformity.
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.short_description: The Wilten collegiate church is one of the first large longitudinal buildings built in the German-speaking region following the Thirty Years’ War. Although the architecture and fittings originate from two different periods, the interior presents a uniform appearance. The strict sequence of altars from the first Early Baroque period of interior design work, framed in gold and black, contrast with the fresco panels from the second phase with their bold colours, framed by heavy Italian ceiling stucco.
90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.dates: 1651–1667: new Baroque building; 1713–1719: façade; 1702/03: stuccowork; 1702–1707: ceiling paintings; 1665: altars (1767/68 altered)

Frodl-Kraft, E., *Tiroler Barockkirchen*, Innsbruck 1955, p. 31f.  
*850 Jahre Prämonstratenser Chorherrenstift Wilten 1138–1988* (commemorative edition), Innsbruck 1988.  
Skalecki, G., *Deutsche Architektur zur Zeit des Dreißigjährigen Krieges*, Regensburg 1989, p. 121f.

90f3066b-8d4a-516e-ae67-cf0eed88b9ef.history: According to records the first church in Wilten dedicated to St. Lawrence dates back to the 6th century. According to legend the monastery was founded in 878 by the giant Haymon. Conferred on the Premonstratensians in 1138, consecration of the collegiate church took place in 1201. Rebuilt in 1288 following a fire, the collapse of a tower in 1644, which severely damaged the church, resulted in the new Baroque building (1651–77). The façade as well as the frescos and stucco ornamentation originate from the early 18th century, further modifications took place in the mid-, i.e. second half of the 18th century. From 1946 to 1956 restoration work repaired war damage from 1944.

912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.name: Dome of the Rock.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.description:
Dome of the Rock is one of the oldest Islamic monuments still standing today. It has a grandiose monumental form representing one of a small number of buildings in the Islamic world that may be chronicled as part of the creation and formation of an Islamic art in general.  
Dome of the Rock is built on an octagonal plan topped by a semi-circular great dome and supported by a circular drum. Four doors, each facing one of the cardinal directions, are built into the walls of the building. The façades are covered with marble panels at the bottom and ceramic (glazed) tiles at the top. These tiles date back to the time of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent who ordered the replacement of the original glass mosaic with ceramic tiles in the period AH 952–9 / AD 1545–52. The marble panels were also renewed several times. The interior or inner drum, the cylinder which carries the dome, is also adorned with glass mosaic tiles. At present the outer dome is covered with gold-plated copper panels, although it was formerly of lead covered with a thin layer of gold-plate.  
Both the interior and exterior of the Dome of the Rock is built on an octagonal plan, surrounding the exalted Rock. According to Islamic belief the Rock is where the Prophet Muhammad ascended to the heavens (*Mi'raj*) on the night of his nocturnal journey from Mecca to Jerusalem *(Isra')*. The interior octagonal (which follows the outer octagon walls) is supported by eight piers and 16 columns. The rotunda is supported by four piers and 12 columns. Between the piers and columns span semi-circular arches, the façades and surfaces of which are decorated with mosaic tiles and colourful epigraphic texts. The rotunda is covered by a double dome. The inner dome has a diameter of 20.44 m, and is considered to be the oldest wooden structure still extant. It is composed of wooden panels that are decorated with written inscriptions and geometric decorations against a stucco background. Sixteen windows open on to the inside of the dome's drum. The drum is adorned with mosaic decorations and inscriptions from the Qur'an; it is enriched by a large number of inscriptions belonging to different restoration projects carried out by Muslim caliphs and sultans, the most famous being those that date to the Umayyad, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The dome is devoid of figurative decoration and exemplifies a response to changing religious orientation.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.short_description: This is the jewel of Islamic architecture and the oldest Islamic monument that has not undergone fundamental changes. It thus provides very important testimony to the creation and formation of Islamic architecture and early Islamic decorative arts. It is also considered to be one of the most beautiful monuments in the world. The building is octagonal in form and is covered on the outside with marble and glazed tilework. The interior is decorated with marble, mosaics, plaster and wood. The great gold dome that towers over the building symbolises Jerusalem.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.method_for_datation: The building is dated by a foundation inscription, written in the *kufic* script. Furthermore, there are a group of early Muslim historians such as al-Maqdisi al-Bishari, the famous geographer (who died at the end of the 4th / 10th century) and who dated the construction of the building to 72 / 691.

The most prominent among them being: the Fatimid caliph, al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36), Sultan Salah al-Din Ayyubi (known as Saladin, r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93) and the Ottoman sultan, Sulayman the Magnificent (r. 926–74 / AD 1520–66).

The name of the craftsman, Muhammad bin Balawar is associated with renovations that took place during the Fatimid era. Mustafa Raqam is linked with the late Ottoman restorations (AH 13th / AD 19th century).

922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.name: Kaftan.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.description:
A woman's garment, rectangular in shape, widening slightly towards the top and open at the front with long, wide sleeves. Braided conical buttons fasten the garment at the top.  
The word 'kaftan' was originally Persian and was adopted by the Ottomans to describe their emperor's dress. It would have been introduced in Morocco by the Sa'did king 'Abd al-Malik (r. AH 984–6 / AD 1576–8), who had lived in Algiers and Istanbul and would have borrowed the word from the Turks. Adopted firstly by the dignitaries and women of the palace, kaftans became fashionable among the middle classes from the late AH 10th / AD 17th century, if the accounts of European travellers are to be believed. Each of the large towns had a particular variation of this type of costume, which would have been covered with a light tunic. Its shape and decoration tell us that this kaftan is from Tetouan. It would not have been hidden under a tunic and would have been worn above a bolero made in the same way and in the same material. Embroidered with gold thread, gold braids and frogging, its arborescent decoration is reminiscent of the designs on the dresses and boleros of Ottoman women in Algeria.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.short_description: This woman's garment is rectangular and slightly opened at the front. It would have been worn above a bolero, and the braided buttons fastened the top of the garment. Its gold thread and gold braiding decoration would have been inspired by the clothes worn by Ottoman women in Algiers.

922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.method_for_datation: This type of kaftan was produced only in Tetouan and was worn only by middle-class women in the north of Morocco.
922e411d-1b69-5d14-ac14-e76be57376fa.method_for_provenance: This type of kaftan was no longer worn at the beginning of the 20th century.

97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.name: Wedding dress
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.short_description: The main fabric of this wedding dress is linen with silk selvedge stripes, with red and yellow taffeta inserts in the sleeves and skirt; the chest panel is couched with gilt cord and yellow, green and purple silk cord, and filled with multi-coloured stain and herringbone stitches. Palestinian weavers used manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled, died and woven in Syria. The Jordanian economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan to participate in those industries. This object shows the diverse population composition of Jordan at that time, through personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

98b84854-315a-5209-aff7-d359b94d60f4.name: Amulet
98b84854-315a-5209-aff7-d359b94d60f4.short_description: This gold amulet case is inscribed on both sides with verses from the Qur’an in an early *kufic* script. The magical-religious properties of amulets are accepted in the Islamic world and are reinforced by the use of verses from the Qur’an. In this case verses are from chapter CXII entitled ‘Sincerity’ extolling God’s purity and devotion to the one God.
keywords: Amulet; Kufic; Quran; Gold; talisman

995266f4-4a66-52c0-aca4-1b45c8cbf765.name: Prayer rug *dhurrie*
995266f4-4a66-52c0-aca4-1b45c8cbf765.description:
In the late 19th and early 20th century, cotton prayer rugs (*dhurrie*) were woven throughout India in rural communities and in town and jail workshops. Cotton was the preferable material as the hot and humid climate of the subcontinent discouraged the use of woollen rugs. Prayer rugs were used for prayer and featured architectural details associated with the mosque - arches, columns and niches that have powerful symbolic meaning, creating a sacred space to concentrate in prayer.  
This multi-arched rug (*saph*) features five architectural niches (*mihrab*) boldly outlined in white on the indigo and navy-blue background.

998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.name: Prayer rug.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.description: A rug produced by peasant weavers in Ghiordes, Anatolia, famous for their tightly woven work with a short, silky wool pile. Ghiordes was one of the major carpet-making centres during the AH 13th / AD 19th century and both the design and colour scheme of this rug, a deep-blue niche framed with elaborate spandrels and borders, is typical of Ghiordes rugs. The niche confirms that this is a prayer rug, used to provide a ritually clean place for the five daily prayers. The niche reflects the *mihrab* or prayer niche in an Islamic mosque, indicating the direction to Mecca, towards which Muslims turn in prayer. It may also symbolise the gateway to Paradise. The ornament suspended in its apex may have a spiritual meaning.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.short_description: Every household in Ghiordes, Anatolia, had a handloom for the womenfolk and girls to weave small carpets and prayer rugs on. This prayer rug is decorated with an elaborate central niche reminiscent of the architectural prayer niche found in Anatolian mosques.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.holder: St. Mungo Museum for Religious Life and Art, Glasgow Museums.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: both the layout and weave of this rug resemble several other 13th- / 19th-century prayer rugs of this type, attributed to Ghiordes in Anatolian Turkey in particular.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

9b83a66c-2937-5afb-80f5-4db5f45d441b.name: Slippers
9b83a66c-2937-5afb-80f5-4db5f45d441b.description: The slippers are handcrafted and embroidered by hand, their unique creation emphasizing their value. This type of footwear demonstrates the influence of oriental art in the technical work of 19th century European artisans, and the great fascination with the objects coming from the East that refer to the luxurious craftsmanship of these countries.

9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.name: Pendant.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.description: A gold crescent-shaped pendant with enamel work. Two bands of delicate gold filigree work surround a panel of cloisonné enamel with a symmetrical design of two birds arranged on either side of a tree. The pendant may have been hung with strings of pearls from the three loops along the bottom. The enamel inset imitates Byzantine designs. Gold jewellery from Byzantium was known in Fatimid Egypt originating either from Byzantine craftsmen who immigrated to Egypt or through diplomatic gifts sent by Byzantine rulers. In 1046 the Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir (r.1036–94) received a large gift from the Emperor of Byzantium which included hundreds of gold vessels, brocade and gold-embroidered turbans. This exchange of diplomatic gifts is recorded in The Book of Treasures and Gifts, by Ibn Zubayr, written just before the destruction and dispersal of the Fatimid treasury in 1062.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.short_description: Gold jewellery with delicate filigree work was popular during the Fatimid period. Some pieces, such as this pendant, also feature enamel work derived from Byzantine designs. The Fatimid treasury is known to have accumulated a vast hoard of gold objects that included jewellery.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_datation: The pendant resembles other gold jewellery from the Fatimid era; generally small in size and often decorated with filigree work, cloisonné enamel, or niello. From the mid-11th century figurative elements began to appear, such as birds. The dating of Fatimid jewellery has been derived from excavations in a number of sites, including that at Fustat in Cairo.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.method_for_provenance: The Fatimids were renowned for their rich splendid jewellery. Most of the workmanship would have taken place in Egypt, the political centre of the Fatimid dynasty.
9cd3c434-a84c-5e25-9be3-4b5d88eaa44c.obtention: Purchased by the British Museum in 1981.

9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.name: Danan Synagogue (Slat Rabbi Shelomo Danan).
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.description:
In order to establish his authority over the country, Mulay Rashid, the founder of the 'Alawid dynasty (AH 1075–83 / AD 1664–72) had to fight against the Marabut brotherhoods, in particular the Dilai, whose *zawiya* was located near to the town of Khenifra in the Middle Atlas on the land of the Ait Ishaq, where a significant Jewish community lived.  
In AH 1076 / AD 1666, Mulay Rashid took Fez from the Dilai and decided to make it his capital. He undertook the revitalisation of the town by restoring it and repopulating it. To do so, he moved in elements of the Arab Cheraga tribe from eastern Morocco, whom he enlisted in his army, and he brought a large part of the Jewish community of Ait Ishaq to relaunch economic activity in the town and take on certain administrative functions. This migration involved the expansion of the Jewish Quarter (*mellah*) and it resulted in the construction of a new synagogue.  
This new temple, erected by Mimon Bussidan around AH 1091 / AD 1680, owes its name to Rabbi Shelomo Danan (1847–1928) who officiated there at the beginning of the 20th century.  
The building originally consisted of three naves backing on to the rampart of the *mellah*, which constitutes its eastern wall and is home to the huge *hekhal*, the cabinet where the Torah scrolls are kept.  
A fourth nave, with a lower ceiling and an *azara* (women's gallery), was added subsequently.  
Later still, the synagogue was endowed with a *teba* (altar) raised up on steps, which included an elegant wooden lectern and a wrought-iron balustrade overlooking the prayer room.  
The entrance, originally located in the enclosure wall, was blocked up at the time of the construction of the fourth nave, and henceforth access was gained from the opposite side through a very plain door, a square hallway that leads to the *teba* and the fourth nave.  
Restoration work undertaken at the end of the 20th century brought to light a *mikvé* (ritual bath) beneath the synagogue, from which a trapdoor leads to an underground water course. The faithful would go there during the festival of Rosh Hashanah to 'to shake off their sins in the water'. This *mikvé*, which was initially located outside the synagogue, was bricked in to enable the construction of the fourth nave.  
The building's load-bearing walls are made of full bricks and lime mortar, with the exception of the eastern wall which is part of the adobe enclosure wall.  
The octagonal pillars are made of full bricks and the floors are covered with green and white rectangular earthenware tiles set in a herringbone pattern.  
The interior decoration is focused around the Torah cabinets, with the upper part being surrounded by a large band of sculpted plaster painted with geometric motifs, and the lower part with a band of ceramic marquetry in white and blue that reaches the floor via a high step that runs all round the room.  
The synagogue is no longer used as a place of worship and, being classified as an historic monument, it is open to the public.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.short_description:
To kickstart the economy and reinforce the government, the 'Alawid Mulay Rashid moved a part of the Middle Atlas Jewish community to Fez, which he had recently conquered. A new synagogue was erected in the extended Jewish quarter.  
The original three naves were later complemented by an altar with a wooden lectern, an iron balustrade, and a fourth nave with a women's gallery. There is a ritual bath in the basement. In the prayer room, the painted plasterwork and ceramic inlays of the Torah cabinets are the main decorative elements.  
The synagogue is no longer sacred and is now open to the public.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.method_for_datation: Information provided by Simon Lévy, General Secretary of the Foundation of Judeo-Moroccan Cultural Heritage.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.bibliography: *La Synagogue Danan restaurée*, Foundation of Judeo-Moroccan Cultural Heritage, Casablanca, undated.
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.patrons: Mimon Bussidan, well-known Jew originally from Zawiyat Aït Ishaq (Middle Atlas).
9d54bf76-910a-5ef1-bcfd-bc844a35cd59.author: Kamal Lakhdar

a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.name: Aleppo Room.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.description:
A prosperous broker and a Christian citizen of the town of Aleppo commissioned the painted panels of the walls of the entrance room in his house at the beginning of the 17th century. The paintings within the Aleppo room thus make up the oldest collection from a Syrian dwelling house from the Ottoman period. The Christian patron engaged craftsmen from the best workshops of the time in his desire for the entrance room, into which his guests would first arrive, to be painted in a variety of themes. These themes were based on contemporary Islamic book illustration, consisting of floral and geometric compositions, rendered in the best traditional Ottoman style. Christian themes from the Old and New Testaments, and the depiction of Mary with Child, sit alongside courtly scenes like those portrayed in Persian book illustration. The selection of encircling Psalms, Arabic proverbs and Persian principles further add to the impression of a peaceful community of different religious beliefs living together.  
The central panels are found in the back part of the main niche, to the left and right of a wall cupboard. Courtly themes are repeated on the left-side panel, including a ruler sitting on a throne, a hunt and a hunting party with a prince holding a falcon. In contrast, Christian themes are portrayed on the right-side panel, and include the Last Supper, Salome’s dance in front of King Herod and the sacrifice of Isaac. Other panels around the room have individual depictions from either courtly or Christian subject matters, such as the love story of Leila and Majnun of Nizami (1141–1202) from the Haft Paykar, or the Virgin Mary and Child or Saint George. Real and imaginary animals are depicted alongside. It is the variety of the themes of these paintings that make these earliest surviving wall panels such a comprehensive collection, a variety that could perhaps only have arisen in the Syrian trading town Aleppo.  
The name Halab Shah ibn Isa, one of the craftsmen, appears on the cornice.  
  
Click [here](https://youtu.be/4toX47mtAIE) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
a248d8b4-e492-5f6d-bdb7-ab94d668d922.short_description: The painted wooden panels belong to the audience room in a house of a Christian merchant in Aleppo, Syria, which is the only surviving example of a painted and dated room from the 17th century. Its ornamental and figural repertoire includes Christian themes as well as Arabic verses.

a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.name: Tile Panel for a Spandrel
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.short_description: Buildings in Isfahan, capital of the Safavid dynasty in the seventeenth century, were lavishly decorated with tilework. An innovation of this period, found in palaces and other secular structures, was the use of individually painted square tiles, which were combined to form a larger pictorial scene and employed the *cuerda seca* technique. First developed in Iran in the later 14th century, *cuerda seca* was designed to produce multicolored glazed tile decoration quickly, efficiently, and cheaply. To prevent the different glazes from running during the (single) firing process, the decorative motifs were outlined with a greasy pigment that burned off in the firing, leaving behind a dull, dark line. This tile panel is half of a pair of spandrels that was once set above an archway in a palatial pavilion known as the Hasht Bihisht, completed in Hegira 1080 / AD 1669-70. Here, amid a tranquil floral landscape filled with birds, a lion attacks a stag, a motif that can perhaps be interpreted as a visualization of a contemporary poetic metaphor for the arrival of spring. Other contemporaneous spandrels from the Hasht Bihisht on the eastern facade include animal combats, for example, a leopard and a gazelle and a tiger and a gazelle.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.method_for_datation: The tile panel is very closely related in terms of style, subject matter (animal combat), technique and dimensions to other spandrels still in situ at the Hasht Bihisht pavilion in Isfahan, which dates to Hegira 1080 / AD 1669-70. It may have come from the western façade of the structure.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.method_for_provenance: The technique, style, and dimensions are consonant with tilework from the Hasht Bihisht.
a488d457-650b-5f4c-b27b-4e2bcbd9ff6d.provenance: Iran, probably Isfahan, Hasht Bihisht, West façade

a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.name: Pendant.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.description:
Archaeological excavations in the Egyptian City of Fustat have furnished us with some pieces of jewellery such as bracelets, rings, earrings and pendants of gold and silver. A number of techniques in jewellery-making and ornamentation were widespread in Egypt during the Fatimid period. Some of the most important techniques were carving, piercing and enamel inlay. The piece illustrated here is a good example of decorative enamel inlay.  
Generally, decorative enamelling was done in one of two ways: one way – called lobed enamel – involves pouring the enamel into small metallic lobes, closely resembling moulds. After firing the lobes in a kiln, they are then mounted in specific places in accordance with the design on to the gold surface of the piece of jewellery. The other way involves making deep-grooved decorative carvings of the desired design on the surface of the piece; enamel is then poured into the grooves and the piece is then fired in a kiln. The former method is a quicker and faster way than the latter. The piece illustrated here is an exquisite example of lobed enamel jewellery – the first method of decoration with enamel.  
This is a circular pendant whose form assumes a concave surface. Its decorative layout is arranged along three horizontal sections. The central section, which is the broadest, is filled with an inscription in *kufic* script set in white, decorated in red, and placed against a background of ash-green. The text reads: “… God is best to take care \[of him\]” and is part of verse (*ayah*) 64 of the Chapter of Joseph (*Yusuf*; no. 12). The sections above and below the inscription are decorated with a vegetal branch, each of which is depicted in red, and set against a green background.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.short_description: Women used all kinds and shapes of jewellery, such as bracelets, rings, earrings, brooches and pendants. Techniques in ornamentation included engraving, incising, piercing and enamel inlay. This piece is good example of decorative enamel inlay.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.method_for_datation: The pendant is dated by means of studying the *kufic* script used in the decoration. Dating was also greatly assisted by a comparative study of the pendant's craftsmanship that, together with some objects made of stucco, have been uncovered in archaeological excavations in the Egyptian City of Fustat, and which are attributed to the same period.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.method_for_provenance: A study of the pendant's craftsmanship with reference to stucco objects also uncovered in archaeological excavations in Fustat suggests that the pendant may have been produced there.
a9696cec-e2a4-5df3-86c8-4f47e45be0d4.obtention: The object was discovered during the course of archaeological excavations that took place in Fustat in 1916.

aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Azulejos
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.alternate_name: *St. Francis of Assisi* Blue-and-white tile panel
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.description:
Our Lady of the Visitation Convent in Vila Verde dos Francos is a Franciscan Convent of the third order and, therefore, part of a noble residence where a few Franciscan friars lived a monastic life. D. António de Noronha, the owner of the residence, along with other nobles – both men and women – often went there to retreat.  
Society life necessarily followed strict social rules, which were taken very seriously. As part of the social mores was the struggle of the Christian soul against the Devil – Psychomachy – fundamental to salvation. Updated continuously up until the end of the Baroque period, the Hagiography (example of life) of St. Francis of Assisi was used as a didactic tale to explain to men, and especially to women, how to behave in society. As shown here, St. Francis was a sinner during his youth and, like him, people have the opportunity to resist temptation.  
The remarkable blue-and-white tile composition, by an artist from the Oliveira Bernardes' workshop circle, reveals a sophisticated technique and an artistic capacity to transform these moralising figurative *azulejos* into impressive iconographic themes.  
Handling the use of engravings in a most creative way, the artist adapted those compositions: pilasters with angels and *albarradas* (vases with flowers), to the wall covering as if it were a scenic architectural stage.  
This particular chancel panel recounts the episode of St. Francis converting Muslims in Syria during the Fifth Crusade. On this journey a woman with a lovely body but a "filthy soul" tried to tempt him. Feigning acceptance of her sinful offer, he took off his clothes and leaped into a fire, inviting her to follow him. He miraculously survived, having overcome the temptation and led the woman to salvation.
aab132c1-e5b3-5bd5-b73f-973fd09a0e8e.short_description: In this *azulejos* panel, St. Francis of Assisi is tempted by Evil, symbol of vanity and lust, one of the most regrettable sins of women. Evil Is conveyed here by a half-naked, half-devil woman.

ab28e47f-1931-5994-aa22-506877f6b7b6.name: Tiara
ab28e47f-1931-5994-aa22-506877f6b7b6.short_description: A richly jewelled Moroccan wedding tiara decorated with emeralds and gemstones and displays a pyramidal shape facet and open back. The gold jewellery of Morocco is often served as gifts associated with royalty and noble ladies and was probably used in wedding ceremonies and would have been worn by both Muslim and Jewish brides. It is inscribed with “honour belongs to God and His Messenger”.

ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.name: Prayer hanging
ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.short_description: Pieced together from numerous embroidered fabric scraps, this cotton hanging is suggestive of a mihrab, or prayer niche. The arched "niche" form at center is formed by juxtaposing light fabrics against dark reds. In the Qur'an, God (Allah) is likened to the presence of a lustrous lamp in a niche. Hence, lamps are often placed in niches in mosques and, similarly, they are depicted in niches on tile panels and textiles. In this textile, two stylized lamps extend outward from the top of the arch.

ab9dbdc1-5022-5a92-be31-a76cf3b05af7.name: Single-volume Qur’an with lacquer-painted binding signed by Lutf ‘Ali Shirazi
ab9dbdc1-5022-5a92-be31-a76cf3b05af7.short_description:
The first two of the three illuminated opening spreads bear an index of *sura* headings and a prayer. The main text begins on the third and is written in a fine, clear *naskhi* which compares well to that of Visal, the pen-name of one of the most highly esteemed calligraphers and poets of 19th-century Iran. The marginal commentaries are signed by Visal’s second son, Mirza Mahmud, pen-named *hakim* (’the physician’), who enjoyed a considerable reputation as a *nasta‘liq* scribe.  
The lacquer covers are the work of Lutf ‘Ali Shirazi, who had close associations with the Visal family. The outer covers are variations on the so-called *gul-u bulbul* (‘flower-and-bird’) theme, with two birds in a rose bush on a sparkling dark-brown ground. The doublures have a superb composition of an iris and other flowers on an imitation tortoise-shell ground. The borders have quotations from *sura* *al-Baqara*, II, verses 255–7 on the front and verse 201, with other religious phrases, on the back.

ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.name: Multiple-niche prayer kilim (*saf*)
ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.description: The multiple-niche prayer carpets, called *saf* (from the Arabic word for “row”), are sometimes improperly referred to as “family” prayer rugs. They were used in mosques, their particular design allowing several people to pray one next to the other. Here, the uneven colour areas in the *mihrab* field, the somewhat irregular shape of the arches, and the stylised vegetal motifs are indicative of its tribal, probably Kurdish, provenance. Unlike most large Anatolian kilims, made of two narrow bands, this one is made of only one piece. The Arabic inscriptions and the fact that the carpet was dated make it all the more valuable.
